title: Carrying capacity: why no population grows for ever, and why hunters and hunted rise and fall

summary.text: One bacterium can split in two in about 20 minutes. If all her daughters kept splitting, they would soon outweigh the Earth. Yet that never happens. In this lesson you will double rice grains square by square, grow a paper forest until it is full, and plot a real island's reindeer.
summary.art: A paper grid of 36 squares half filled with beans, a pair of dice beside it, and a hand-drawn line graph that rises steeply and then flattens.

intro.hook: Put one grain of rice on the table today. Tomorrow put two, the next day four, and double it every day. On which day would you need more rice than a whole one-kilogram packet holds? Guess the day, and say why you think so.
intro.text: A one-kilogram packet holds roughly 50,000 grains. Most people guess a day far too late. In the first activity, Doubling Rice, you find the real day with real grains. Living beings multiply in the same doubling way. So here is the question for this lesson. If every living being can double, why is the world not buried in bacteria, or rats, or deer? What stops them, and at what number?
intro.art: A child at a table placing rice grains in small heaps of 1, 2, 4 and 8, looking at an unopened packet of rice with a question mark above it.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a population is, and name the four things that change its number.
By the end I can explain, using Doubling Rice, why doubling cannot go on for ever.
By the end I can say what a limiting factor and a carrying capacity are, using my Full Island Test results.
By the end I can draw and read four shapes of population graph: the J, the S, the overshoot and crash, and the wave.
By the end I can explain why predator and prey numbers rise and fall, and why the predator's peak comes later.
By the end I can explain how scientists count animals they cannot see all at once.
By the end I can say what changes a carrying capacity, give real examples, and say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: A population is all the members of one species who live in one place at one time.
terms.example: All the house crows of Chennai are one population. All the chital of Mudumalai are another.
terms.art: A flock of house crows on the wires of one street, with a dotted line drawn round the whole flock.

terms.meaning: The birth rate is how many young are born in a population in one year. The death rate is how many members die in one year.
terms.example: If 20 kids are born in a goat herd in a year and 5 goats die, the herd grows by 15.
terms.art: A herd of goats with a few small kids on one side and a plus sign, and a few faded goats on the other side with a minus sign.

terms.meaning: Immigration is members arriving from another place. Emigration is members leaving for another place.
terms.example: A young male tiger who walks from one forest to another emigrates from the first and immigrates into the second.
terms.art: A young tiger walking along a strip of trees from one patch of forest to another, with an arrow along his path.

terms.meaning: Exponential growth is growth by multiplying. The number is multiplied by the same amount in each equal step of time, for example doubled.
terms.example: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 is exponential growth. Each number is double the one before.
terms.art: Heaps of rice grains in a row, each heap twice the size of the one before.

terms.meaning: The doubling time is how long a population takes to become twice as big.
terms.example: Some bacteria in warm, rich food have a doubling time of about 20 minutes.
terms.art: One rod-shaped bacterium becoming two, then four, with a small clock showing 20 minutes between each step.

terms.meaning: A limiting factor is anything a population needs that is in short supply, or anything that removes its members. It holds the number down.
terms.example: For mosquitoes in a dry month, the limiting factor is still water for their eggs.
terms.art: A dry street with one small puddle in a coconut shell and a few mosquitoes crowded over it.

terms.meaning: The carrying capacity of a place is the largest number of one species that the place can keep alive year after year. At that number the place is not damaged.
terms.example: A meadow that grows enough grass for 800 tahr through the dry months has a carrying capacity of about 800 tahr.
terms.art: A hillside of grass with a herd of mountain goats spread across it and a dotted line across a graph above them marked 'limit'.

terms.meaning: An S-shaped curve is the graph of a population that grows slowly, then fast, then slowly again, and levels off at the carrying capacity. Scientists also call it logistic growth.
terms.example: The line graph from the Full Island Test is an S-shaped curve.
terms.art: A line graph shaped like a stretched letter S, flattening under a dotted line.

terms.meaning: A J-shaped curve is the graph of a population that keeps multiplying with nothing yet holding it back. It bends upward more and more steeply.
terms.example: Rabbits set free in Australia in the 1800s grew on a J-shaped curve for their first decades there.
terms.art: A line graph that starts flat and bends sharply upward like the letter J.

terms.meaning: An overshoot happens when a population grows past the carrying capacity. The members then eat or use up more than the place can grow back.
terms.example: Reindeer on St Matthew Island overshot. They ate the slow-growing lichen faster than it could grow back.
terms.art: A line graph rising above a dotted limit line, with bare ground drawn under the top of the curve.

terms.meaning: A crash is a fast fall in a population, when many members die in a short time.
terms.example: After the overshoot, the reindeer on St Matthew Island crashed from about 6,000 to 42.
terms.art: A line graph falling steeply from a high peak almost to zero.

terms.meaning: Population density is how many members live in a fixed area. It tells you how crowded they are.
terms.example: Ten tigers in 100 square kilometres is a high density for tigers.
terms.art: Two equal squares of forest, one with two deer in it and one with twenty.

terms.meaning: A density-dependent factor is a limit that presses harder when a population is more crowded.
terms.example: A disease spreads faster in a crowded herd, because sick and healthy members meet more often.
terms.art: A crowded herd of deer with a few drawn in a paler colour to show they are ill, close to the healthy ones.

terms.meaning: A predator is an animal who hunts and eats other animals. The prey is the animal who is hunted.
terms.example: A rat snake is a predator of field rats. The rats are her prey.
terms.art: A rat snake in a paddy field looking toward a rat among the stalks.

terms.meaning: A population cycle is a rise and fall in number that repeats again and again, with about the same time between peaks.
terms.example: In northern Canada the number of snowshoe hares peaks about every ten years.
terms.art: A line graph shaped like a row of waves, with the peaks evenly spaced.

terms.meaning: A time lag is a delay between a cause and its effect.
terms.example: Predators become many only after their prey has become many. The gap between the two peaks is the time lag.
terms.art: Two wavy lines on one graph, the second with each peak a little to the right of the first, and a small double arrow between two peaks.

terms.meaning: A refuge is a place where prey are safe from their predators.
terms.example: Burrows, thorn bushes and thick grass are refuges for field rats.
terms.art: A rat disappearing into a burrow under a thorn bush while a snake waits outside.

terms.meaning: A sample is a small part of a group that you count or measure. From it you work out something about the whole group.
terms.example: Forty beans taken from a big bowl without looking are a sample of the beans in the bowl.
terms.art: A hand lifting a small cup of beans out of a large bowl of beans.

terms.meaning: Mark and recapture is a way to estimate a population. You mark some members, let them mix back in, and see what share of a later sample is marked.
terms.example: Tigers are told apart by their stripes in camera photos. The stripes are their marks.
terms.art: Two camera photos of tigers side by side with circles drawn round matching stripe patterns.

terms.meaning: A sustainable yield is an amount you can take from a population every year without making the population smaller.
terms.example: If a pond's fish add 9 new fish each year, catching 9 each year is a sustainable yield.
terms.art: A fishing net lifting a few fish from a pond that still holds many fish.

explanations.concept: A population, and the four ways its number changes
explanations.definition: A population is all the members of one species who live in one place at one time. Its number changes in only four ways: births, deaths, members arriving and members leaving.
explanations.description: Scientists do not study 'tigers' in general. They study the tigers of one forest, because those tigers share the same food and meet each other. That group is a population. Births and arrivals make it bigger. Deaths and departures make it smaller. If more are added than removed, the population grows. If the two match, the number stays the same, even though the members keep changing. So every question about a population comes down to one thing. What is changing the births, the deaths, the arrivals or the departures?
examples: The house sparrows of one street in Madurai are a population. A sparrow who moves to the next street has emigrated.
A pot of curd holds a population of bacteria. No bacteria arrive or leave, so only births and deaths change their number.
India's tiger numbers are worked out one forest at a time, because each forest holds its own population.
explanations.art: A circle of forest with four arrows: young born inside, old animals fading inside, one animal walking in and one walking out.

explanations.concept: Doubling: why growth by multiplying is so fast
explanations.definition: Exponential growth is growth by multiplying. When each member leaves more than one young who lives, the population is multiplied by the same amount in each generation.
explanations.description: Growth by adding is steady: 2, 4, 6, 8. Growth by multiplying starts slowly and then races: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Why does a living population multiply and not add? Because the young grow up and have young of their own. Every new member is also a new parent. A bacterium splits into two, and both daughters split again. In warm, rich food, the gut bacterium Escherichia coli can do this about every 20 minutes. Starting from one cell, that would be more than the weight of the Earth in about two days. This sum is true, and it has never happened. So something always stops the doubling. On a graph, growth by multiplying makes a J-shaped curve.
examples: In Doubling Rice, square 11 needed 1,024 grains and square 17 needed more than a one-kilogram packet.
European rabbits were set free in Australia in the 1800s. Within some decades they had spread across most of the continent.
Milk left out on a warm day turns sour within hours, because the bacteria in it double again and again.
explanations.art: A row of squares with rice heaps doubling from one grain to a heap spilling over its square.

explanations.concept: Limiting factors: what holds a number down
explanations.definition: A limiting factor is anything a population needs that is in short supply, or anything that removes its members.
explanations.description: Every living being needs energy, water, certain atoms such as nitrogen, and a place to live. When any one of these runs short, fewer young are born or more members die. The main limiting factors are food, water, space, light for plants, nesting places, predators, disease and the members' own waste. Why does only one factor matter at a time? Because growth stops at the first need that runs out, even if all the others are plentiful. A crop with plenty of water and sunlight still stays small if the soil has too little nitrogen. The German farm scientist Carl Sprengel wrote this in 1828, and the chemist Justus von Liebig made it famous in 1840. It is called the law of the minimum.
examples: Yeast in sugar water slows down as the sugar runs out and as the alcohol the yeast makes builds up.
In a city, pigeons are limited mostly by food. Where people scatter grain every day, there are more pigeons.
Under a thick banyan, almost no seedlings grow, because the limiting factor there is light.
explanations.art: A potted plant with a full watering can and bright sun beside it, but pale small leaves, and an empty bag labelled 'nitrogen'.

explanations.concept: Carrying capacity and the S-shaped curve
explanations.definition: The carrying capacity of a place is the largest number of one species that the place can keep alive year after year. At that number the place is not damaged. A population that grows up to it and levels off makes an S-shaped curve.
explanations.description: In the Full Island Test, the forest began by nearly doubling. Then more and more seeds landed on squares that already had a tree, and those seeds died. At 36 trees every seed died, and the number stopped. Nothing told the trees to stop. Each tree did the same thing in every round. The number stopped because the island had 36 squares. That number, 36, was the island's carrying capacity. Scientists write it as the letter K. The Belgian mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst described this S-shaped growth in the 1830s and 1840s and named it logistic growth. In 1934 the Russian biologist Georgy Gause grew yeast and tiny pond animals in glass tubes. He counted them every day, and their numbers followed the S-shaped curve. Our test is simpler than a real forest. Real trees die, and real seeds can wait in the soil.
examples: Curd sets overnight and then stops getting much more sour. The bacteria have used much of the milk sugar, and their own acid slows them.
The rhinos of Kaziranga were about a dozen in 1908. In 2022 the count was 2,613, and it rose by only 200 in the four years before.
On the half island, the forest levelled off near 18 trees, because there were only 18 squares.
explanations.art: A line graph shaped like a stretched S that flattens under a dotted line labelled K, beside a grid of 36 squares full of beans.

explanations.concept: Why growth is fastest in the middle
explanations.definition: A population adds the most new members when it is about half way to its carrying capacity.
explanations.description: Look at your Full Island table. In the first rounds almost every seed lived, but there were few trees to drop seeds. In the last rounds there were many trees, but almost every seed died. In the middle there were many parents and still many empty squares. That is when the most new trees were added in one round. Two things are multiplied together here: the number of parents, and the share of young who find room. The first goes up as the second goes down. Their product is largest in the middle. This matters to anyone who harvests a wild population. A fish population that is kept near half its carrying capacity adds the most new fish each year. This is a result of the simple model. Real fish populations are harder to measure, so real fishing rules need a safety margin.
examples: On the 36-square island, the biggest gain in one round came when there were about 18 trees.
A full pond adds almost no new fish. A nearly empty pond also adds few. A half-full pond adds the most.
A bamboo clump spreads fastest after it is well grown but before the clumps touch each other.
explanations.art: A hill-shaped graph of 'new trees added' against 'trees on the island', with the top of the hill above the number 18.

explanations.concept: Limits that press harder in a crowd
explanations.definition: A density-dependent factor is a limit that presses harder when a population is more crowded. A density-independent factor acts the same whether the members are few or many.
explanations.description: Why does a population settle near one number, and not drift anywhere? Because some limits grow stronger as the crowd grows. When members are crowded, each one gets less food. Disease passes more easily, because sick and healthy members meet more often. Predators gather where prey is easy to find. So in a crowd, births fall and deaths rise, and the number comes down. When members are few, each gets plenty, and the number goes up. This pushes the population back toward the carrying capacity from both sides. Other events do not care about crowding. A cyclone, a frost or a forest fire kills a share of the members whether they are few or many. Those events knock a population down, but they do not hold it at one number.
examples: In a crowded poultry shed, one sick hen can pass an illness to hundreds. In a small backyard flock the illness often stops.
A cyclone on the Odisha coast fells coconut palms in thick groves and thin groves alike.
In the Meadow Game, disease struck only herds of nine or more.
explanations.art: Two pens of hens, one crowded and one with few hens, with wavy lines showing an illness spreading quickly through the crowded pen.

explanations.definition: An overshoot happens when a population grows past the carrying capacity. If the members damage what they live on, the number then falls very fast, which is called a crash.
explanations.description: In 1944, 29 reindeer were put on St Matthew Island, off Alaska. The island had thick lichen, which reindeer eat in winter, and no wolves. By 1957 there were about 1,350 reindeer, and in 1963 about 6,000. In the winter that followed, nearly all of them died. In 1966 the biologist David Klein counted 42 living reindeer among thousands of skeletons. Why did the number not level off gently, as in the Full Island Test? Because lichen grows back very slowly, over many years. The reindeer could keep multiplying on the stored lichen of past years after they had passed the number the island could feed. The limit arrived late, and all at once. Scientists agree on these counts. They do not fully agree on the cause of the deaths.
examples: Yeast in a closed bottle of sugar water multiply, then die off when the sugar is gone and the alcohol is strong.
In Mizoram, rats multiply when the bamboo fruits, and die back when the fruit is finished.
Chital brought to the Andaman Islands by the British have no large predators there. Studies find fewer young plants where the deer are many.

perspectives.who: David Klein, who counted the reindeer in 1957, 1963 and 1966
perspectives.explanation: The herd had eaten the lichen down. The reindeer went into the hard winter of 1963 to 1964 thin and short of food. The overshoot and the weather together caused the crash.

perspectives.who: Later researchers who studied the weather records of that winter
perspectives.explanation: The winter was one of the worst on record, with deep snow and strong winds. They argue that the weather was the main cause, and that many reindeer would have died even with more lichen.

explanations.art: A line graph climbing steeply past a dotted limit line and then dropping almost to zero, above a bare island with a few reindeer.

explanations.concept: Carrying capacity is not one fixed number
explanations.definition: The carrying capacity of a place is not fixed. It changes with the seasons and with the weather from year to year. It also changes with what other living beings, including people, do to the place.
explanations.description: A hillside grows much more grass in the monsoon than in the dry months. So which season sets the carrying capacity? The hardest one. A herd must get through the hungriest weeks of the year, so the food of those weeks sets the number. A year of good rain raises the capacity, and a drought lowers it. Other species change it too. More deer on the same grass means less for each herd. People raise the capacity for some species and lower it for others. A rubbish heap raises it for street dogs and crows. A cut forest lowers it for hornbills. This is why scientists treat carrying capacity as a number that moves, and why real populations wobble around it.
examples: After a good monsoon in Rajasthan, there are more blackbuck fawns the next year.
Open rubbish in a city raises the carrying capacity for rats, crows and street dogs.
On the half island, the capacity fell from 36 to 18 when half the squares were taken away.
explanations.art: The same hillside drawn twice, green and thick in the monsoon with many deer, and brown and thin in the dry season with few.

explanations.concept: Predator and prey: why the numbers rise and fall
explanations.definition: When a predator depends mostly on one kind of prey, the two numbers can rise and fall again and again. The predator's peak comes after the prey's peak.
explanations.description: In the Rats and Snakes Game, the rats multiplied first, because one snake caught few of them. With many rats, each snake caught enough to live and to raise young. So the snakes multiplied next. Many snakes then caught rats faster than the rats could breed, and the rats fell. With few rats, most snakes caught too little and died. With few snakes, the rats began to rise again. Why is the predator always late? Because predators can multiply only after there is plenty of prey, and raising young takes time. And they starve only after the prey has already fallen. This delay is called a time lag. The delay is what keeps the two numbers swinging. In 1925 and 1926 Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra each wrote equations for this, and the equations make two waves, one behind the other.
examples: Fur traders' records from Canada show hare numbers peaking about every ten years, with lynx peaking a year or two later.
In a paddy field, rat snakes and owls become more common a season after the rats do.
Ladybird beetles arrive on a rose bush after the aphids have multiplied, and leave after the aphids are eaten.
explanations.art: Two wavy lines on one graph, a taller one for rats and a lower one for snakes, with each snake peak a little to the right of a rat peak.

explanations.definition: Scientists still test what drives the rise and fall of hares and other animals with cycles. It may be their predators, their food, or both together.
explanations.description: The simple story says the predator alone drives the waves. Real populations are less tidy. In the Yukon in Canada, Charles Krebs and his team fenced large areas of forest for eight years. In some they gave the hares extra food. In some they kept out lynx and coyotes. In some they did both. Extra food alone raised hare numbers, and so did fewer predators alone. Doing both raised them far more than the two effects added together. So the hares' own food and their predators act together. On Isle Royale, an island in a North American lake, scientists have counted wolves and moose every winter since 1958. The two numbers do swing, but not in neat waves. Hard winters, ticks and the wolves' small family tree have all changed the counts.
examples: On Isle Royale the wolves fell to two animals by 2016. Nineteen wolves were brought in during 2018 and 2019, and by the 2026 winter count there were 37.
In India, the number of tigers a forest holds follows the number of deer, pigs and gaur there.
Many populations do not cycle at all. Most birds and large mammals stay near one number.

perspectives.explanation: Predators cause the hare cycle. Most hares that die in the falling years are killed by lynx, coyotes, owls and hawks.
At the peak the hares eat the best twigs, and the plants that are left are poor food. Hungry hares breed less and are easier to catch.
Neither alone explains it. Food and predators together had a much bigger effect than either one. The cycle comes from three levels acting on each other: plants, hares and predators.

explanations.art: A fenced square of snowy forest with hares inside and a lynx outside the fence looking in.

explanations.concept: Why hunter and hunted do not wipe each other out
explanations.definition: Prey survive alongside their predators when some prey are always out of reach, in refuges or in places the predators have not found yet.
explanations.description: If a predator is very good at hunting, why does she not eat every last prey animal and then starve? In a small, simple space, that is exactly what happens. Georgy Gause put a hunting pond animal called Didinium in a tube with her prey, Paramecium. The hunters ate every one and then starved. When he gave the prey a place to hide, some prey lived on. When he added a few new animals of each kind every few days, the numbers rose and fell in waves. In 1958 Carl Huffaker tried with two kinds of mites on trays of oranges. In a simple tray, the hunting mites ate all the prey mites and died. When he made the tray large and patchy, with sticky barriers that slowed the hunters, the two rose and fell three times. So lasting waves need a world with hiding places and distance.
examples: Field rats have burrows. Deer have thick lantana and steep slopes. Small fish have weeds.
In the Rats and Snakes Game, a new snake and new rats 'arrive from the next field' when one side dies out. Without that rule the game soon ends.
A tank with one big fish and a few small ones needs plants, or the small fish are all eaten.
explanations.art: A tray of oranges with tiny mites on some of them and thin lines of petroleum jelly between the oranges.

explanations.concept: Counting a population you cannot see all at once
explanations.definition: Scientists estimate a population from samples. In mark and recapture, they mark some members, let them mix back in, and see what share of a later sample is marked.
explanations.description: Nobody can line up all the tigers of a forest and count them. In Count Without Counting, you marked 40 beans and mixed them back into the bowl. Then you took a new sample. If a quarter of that sample was marked, then your 40 marked beans were about a quarter of the bowl. So the bowl held about 160. Tigers carry their own marks, because no two tigers have the same stripes. In the 1990s the scientist K. Ullas Karanth set automatic cameras on forest paths at Nagarahole in Karnataka. He treated each photograph as a capture. India's national tiger estimate now uses the same idea. In 2022 it used cameras at more than 32,000 places and estimated about 3,682 tigers. An estimate is not an exact count. That is why the report also gives a range, from about 3,167 to 3,925.
examples: Fish in a tank are estimated by netting some, clipping a tiny mark on a fin, and netting again later.
The Nilgiri tahr of Eravikulam are counted each April by teams who walk every block of the park on the same days.
To estimate the ants of a nest, scientists mark some with a dot of paint and count the share of marked ants later.
explanations.art: A camera strapped to a tree on a forest path taking a picture of a passing tiger, with two photos beside it showing the same stripe pattern.

explanations.concept: How many people can the Earth carry?
explanations.definition: Nobody knows one number for how many people the Earth can carry. The number depends on how people live.
explanations.description: People are animals, and the same four things change our number. There were about 1 billion people around 1804, and 8 billion in November 2022. The second billion took more than a hundred years to add. The eighth took about eleven. The growth is now slowing, mainly because families are having fewer children. In India a woman has about 2 children on average, according to the national health survey of 2019 to 2021. The United Nations expects the world's number to peak at about 10.3 billion in the 2080s. Does the Earth have a carrying capacity for people? In 1995 the scientist Joel Cohen collected the estimates that others had published. They ranged from under 1 billion to more than 1,000 billion. The estimates differ so much because the answer depends on how people choose to live.
examples: A person who eats mostly plants needs much less farmland than a person who eats meat every day.
Fertiliser, canals and new seeds raised the amount of rice and wheat an acre can grow. That raised the Earth's capacity for people.
A family uses the land and water of many far places, through the food, cloth and fuel they buy.

perspectives.explanation: People multiply faster than food can be increased. So hunger and disease will always hold the number down.
When people become crowded, they invent better ways to farm. More people can mean more food from the same land, so the limit moves.
On a finite planet, the use of soil, water and fuel cannot grow for ever. If it overshoots what the Earth renews, the fall can be sudden.
There is no single number. It depends on what people eat, what they throw away, and how fairly they share. Those are choices, so science alone cannot answer the question.

explanations.art: A world map with a rising line graph across it that begins to flatten at its right-hand end.

explanations.concept: Under every limit: energy and atoms
explanations.definition: In the end, a population is limited by two things in the place where its members live. One is the flow of energy. The other is the supply of certain atoms.
explanations.description: Follow any limiting factor down and you reach energy or atoms. Food is energy caught from sunlight by plants, with atoms of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus built in. A square metre of ground receives only so much sunlight in a year, and a plant catches only a small part of it. Each eater passes on only about a tenth of the energy to the next eater. So a place can hold many plants, fewer plant eaters and very few hunters. The Earth as a whole receives a fixed amount of sunlight. That sets a ceiling on almost all the life it can hold at one time. A little life near hot vents in the deep sea runs on chemical energy from rocks instead. No living being can multiply past the energy and atoms that reach them. This is why the doubling sum for bacteria can never come true.
examples: A tiger needs about 50 large prey animals a year, so a forest with few deer can hold very few tigers.
Farm ponds turn green when fertiliser washes in, because nitrogen and phosphorus were the limit for the algae.
The open ocean far from land holds little life, because the water there has very little iron and nitrogen.
explanations.art: Sunlight falling on a patch of grass, with a wide band of grass, a narrower band of deer and one tiger drawn as steps of a pyramid.

explanations.concept: Bacteria sense how crowded they are
explanations.definition: Many bacteria release a chemical signal and sense how much of it is around them. This tells them how many of their own kind are near. It is called quorum sensing.
explanations.description: In 1970 Kenneth Nealson, Terry Platt and Woodland Hastings studied a sea bacterium who can make light. A few of these bacteria in a flask stayed dark. When they became crowded, they all began to glow together. Each bacterium gives off a little of a signal chemical. In a crowd the chemical builds up, and the bacteria sense it and change what they do. Bonnie Bassler and others later showed that very many kinds of bacteria do this. So bacteria take a kind of count of themselves and decide together. A population is not only pushed about by hunger and enemies. Its members also sense each other. Some scientists describe this as chemistry switching genes on and off, with no deciding in it.
examples: The glowing bacteria live inside a small squid, who uses their light to hide her shadow on moonlit nights.
Some bacteria that cause illness wait until they are many before they attack, and they find out by quorum sensing.
Bacteria on your teeth build a slimy coat together, and signals between them help them do it.
explanations.art: A flask of sea water drawn twice, dark with a few bacteria in it and glowing blue-green when crowded with many.

agreed.text: No population can grow by multiplying for ever. Sooner or later something its members need runs short.
agreed.evidence: Every population ever followed, from yeast in a tube to reindeer on an island, has slowed, stopped or crashed. The doubling sum shows why it must.

agreed.text: A population's number changes only through births, deaths, arrivals and departures.
agreed.evidence: Animals have been counted over many years, such as the wolves and moose of Isle Royale since 1958. Every change in such counts can be explained by these four.

agreed.text: In a simple, closed space, a growing population follows an S-shaped curve and levels off.
agreed.evidence: Georgy Gause counted yeast and Paramecium in glass tubes every day in the early 1930s. Many laboratories have repeated this since.

agreed.text: Crowding raises deaths or lowers births in most populations that have been studied closely.
agreed.evidence: Field studies of birds, deer, fish and insects find fewer surviving young per parent in crowded years than in sparse years.

agreed.text: The number of large predators in a place depends on the number of their prey.
agreed.evidence: At 11 sites across India, the measured tiger density rose with the measured density of deer, pigs and wild cattle (Karanth and others, 2004).

agreed.text: Predators and prey last together only where some prey are always out of reach.
agreed.evidence: Gause's tubes in the 1930s and Huffaker's trays of oranges in 1958 both showed this. With no hiding places, the hunters ate all the prey and starved.

challenging.claim: Nature is in balance, so the numbers of wild animals stay the same.
challenging.who: A very old and common belief
challenging.for: Many populations of birds and large mammals do stay near one number for years, as the tahr of Eravikulam have.
challenging.against: Hares, lemmings, locusts and rats rise and crash. Even steady populations wobble with the weather. A steady number is held there by births and deaths that keep changing, not by stillness.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea of a 'balance of nature', where every number stays the same.

challenging.claim: Weather, not crowding, decides the numbers of most animals.
challenging.who: The Australian ecologists Herbert Andrewartha and Charles Birch, 1954
challenging.for: They studied tiny insects called thrips on roses for years. Rain and heat explained most of the rises and falls. The insects were rarely crowded.
challenging.against: Weather can knock a number down, but it cannot hold a number near one level. Most ecologists now think both act: weather shakes the number, and crowding pulls it back.
challenging.context: This card is about what limits a population most: the weather, or the crowding of its own members.

challenging.claim: More people will always mean more hunger.
challenging.for: A population can multiply, while farmland can only be added to. Famines have happened where people outgrew their food.
challenging.against: Since 1798 the number of people has grown about eight times, and food per person has grown too. Ester Boserup showed in 1965 that crowded farmers find ways to grow more. But soil, water and a steady climate are not without limit.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a growing number of people must always run out of food.

challenging.claim: The best way to have fewer pests is to kill as many as you can.
challenging.who: Common sense, and many pest sprayers
challenging.for: Killing does lower the number for a while.
challenging.against: If the food and breeding places stay, the survivors have plenty and multiply back to the same carrying capacity. Taking away the standing water lowers the capacity for mosquitoes, and that lasts.
challenging.context: This card is about two ways to have fewer mosquitoes or rats: killing them, or changing the place.

challenging.claim: A carrying capacity is a tidy idea on paper. Real places do not have one.
challenging.for: Rain, fire and other species change the limit every year. In many places the population never reaches it, so it cannot be measured.
challenging.against: Even a limit that moves is still a limit. The idea explains why a herd left alone does not fill the hillside. It works best as a range, not as one number.
challenging.context: This card is about whether carrying capacity is something real in a place, or only a helpful idea.

big_questions.q: In the Full Island Test the forest stopped at 36. Was the number 36 a fact about the trees, or about the island?
big_questions.hint: What happened to the number when you halved the island but kept the same trees?

big_questions.q: A tigress has cubs and the deer are few. Is 'too many tigers' a fact about tigers, or about deer?
big_questions.hint: Think of what you would have to count to know.

big_questions.q: The rats fed the snakes, and the snakes held back the rats. Which of the two was in charge?
big_questions.hint: Look at your graph from the Rats and Snakes Game. Does one line ever move without the other?

big_questions.q: If a population has no number that it stays at, what do we mean when we say a species is 'doing well'?
big_questions.hint: Think of the hares in Canada, whose number changes tenfold and back in ten years.

big_questions.q: The Earth's limit for people depends on how people live. So who should decide how people live?
big_questions.hint: A person who uses a lot leaves less room for others, including other species.

big_questions.q: When people raise the carrying capacity for themselves, what happens to the capacity for everyone else?
big_questions.hint: Think of a forest turned into a paddy field. Who gained room, and who lost it?

big_questions.q: Bacteria sense how many of them there are. Is a population a crowd of separate beings, or one being with many bodies?
big_questions.hint: Think of the bacteria who glow only together, and of a beehive or an ant nest.

story.title: The Count on the Hill
story.note: A made-up story set in a real place. Eravikulam National Park, near Munnar in Kerala, is real, and so are its Nilgiri tahr, who are wild mountain goats found only in the hills of South India. The park does close in February and March, when the kids are born, and the tahr are counted each April. The 2025 count was 841 tahr in the park, 827 the year before, and 894 in 2014, with more than a hundred kids born in a year. Ponni, her mother Selvi, her cousin Karthik and what they say and do are imagined.
text: Ponni kept the numbers in the back of her maths notebook, where nobody would look.

Her amma, Selvi, was a watcher at Eravikulam. Every April the watchers and the forest officers walked the whole park for several days and counted the tahr. Every April, Amma came home with sore feet and a number, and Ponni wrote the number down.

This year Ponni was ten, and for the first time she had a second number. In March, while the park was closed to visitors, Amma had taken her up the Rajamala road to see the new kids. They were the colour of wet sand, and they jumped on rocks that Ponni would not have climbed for money. The officers said more than a hundred had been born on the hills that season.
So Ponni had done the sum herself. Last April, a little over eight hundred tahr. Add more than a hundred kids. This April there should be well over nine hundred.
Amma came home on the last evening and sat down on the step to pull off her boots.
'How many?' said Ponni.
'A little over eight hundred,' said Amma. 'Fourteen more than last year.'
Ponni looked at her notebook. 'That is wrong,' she said. 'You have missed a hundred.'
Amma laughed, but not unkindly. 'We walked every block. Two teams, every slope. We did not miss a hundred tahr, Ponni. They are not small.'
'Then where are the kids?'
Amma rubbed her foot and did not answer. That was her way. When Ponni asked a question that had a long answer, Amma waited to see how far Ponni would get on her own.

Her cousin Karthik was staying that week, down from Coimbatore. He was twelve and had opinions. 'Somebody is stealing them,' he said. 'Or the count is lazy. Eight hundred, every year? Nothing stays the same every year. In ten years there should be thousands. The whole of Munnar should be full of goats.'
'Tahr,' said Ponni.
'Goats,' said Karthik.

The next morning Amma had to check a path on the high slope, and she took them both. They climbed for two hours through grass that came up to Ponni's knees. It was green now. The first summer showers had come.
'In March this was the colour of a coir mat,' said Amma. 'In January it had frost on it.'

Near a stream they found a tahr lying under a rock ledge. Karthik thought she was asleep. She was very old, a female with a grey muzzle, and she had died some days before. Ponni did not want to look, and then she looked. Amma crouched and gently lifted the lip with a stick.
'See her teeth,' she said. They were worn almost flat. 'She could not grind dry grass any more. In the green months she managed. She did not get through the dry ones.'
Further up, on a path, there was a dropping full of hair, pale and stiff as bristles. 'Leopard,' said Amma. 'That is a kid's hair.'
Karthik had gone quiet. Ponni was counting something in her head, but it was not tahr.

At the top they sat on a rock and ate lemon rice from a steel box. Below them a herd of thirty or forty tahr grazed on a slope so steep it looked like a wall. The kids of this year stayed close to their mothers. There were not as many as Ponni remembered from March.
'Amma,' she said slowly. 'How much grass is there in January?'
'Ah,' said Amma, and put down her spoon.

'Because that is the real count,' said Ponni. 'Not the tahr. The grass. In the rains there is enough here for many more. But they have to get through January too. However many are born, the hill only feeds about eight hundred through the dry months. So the old ones die, and the weak kids, and the leopard takes some. And in April you count what the hill kept.'
'Then the forest department should bring fodder in January,' said Karthik. 'Lorries of it. Then you would have your thousands.'
Ponni thought about that. It sounded right, and it annoyed her that she could not at once say why it was not.

'And the year after?' she said at last. 'The thousands have kids. So you bring more lorries. And they eat this slope bare in between, because there are too many feet on it. And the first year the lorries do not come...' She did not finish.
Amma was looking at her with an expression Ponni had not seen before.

'There is one way to have more tahr,' Amma said. 'More hill. They once lived all along these mountains. The grasslands were planted over with tea and with wattle trees. Where a grassland is given back, the tahr can come back to it. That is the only kind of rise that lasts.'
They walked down in the afternoon. That night Ponni opened the back of her maths notebook. She crossed out 'TAHR' at the top of the page.
She wrote 'WHAT THE HILL CAN FEED'. Then she wrote this year's number under it, the same as before.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns when Ponni stops asking where the kids went and asks how much grass there is in January. A population's number is set by what the place can give in its hardest season. That number is the carrying capacity. Births above it are matched by deaths. Feeding a herd past the capacity only postpones a bigger fall. More living room is what raises the number for good. Let your child find this from the questions, not from you.
ask: More than a hundred kids were born, yet the count hardly changed. What does that tell you about deaths on the hill that year?
Why does January matter more than the rainy months for the number of tahr?
What would happen in the years after, if lorries of fodder were brought every January?
What is the one change that would let more tahr live in these hills for good, and why?
Is there a place near you where the number of some animal seems to stay the same every year? What might be holding it there?

games.title: The Meadow Game: how many chital should stay?
games.context: This is a dice game about a herd of chital, who are spotted deer, on one meadow. The meadow can feed 12. Each year you choose how many chital stay and how many leave to start new herds. You try to send out as many as you can in ten years.

printables.title: A meadow for each player: 12 grass squares in 3 rows of 4, and a circle beside them marked 'new herds'
The year card: what each roll of the die means
items: 1: Drought. This year the meadow feeds only 6.
6: Disease. A herd of 9 or more loses half. A smaller herd loses none.
Too many for the grass? The extra chital die, and 2 more with them.

rules: Each player draws a meadow of 12 squares and puts 3 beans on it. Each bean is a chital. One bean sits on one square.
A turn is one year, and it has three parts. First, fawns are born: add 1 bean for every 2 chital on your meadow. With 3 chital you add 1. With 8 you add 4.
Second, you may send any number of chital away to start new herds. Move those beans into your 'new herds' circle. They are safe there and they score.
Third, roll the die and read the year card. Do what it says.
Last, count your herd. If there are more chital than the meadow can feed this year, the extra ones die. Two more die as well, because the grass was eaten down to the roots.
After ten years, add the beans in your circle to the beans on your meadow. The highest total wins. If you play alone, 25 or more is a strong score.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a grid of 12 squares in 3 rows of 4 and a circle drawn beside it, with 3 beans on the grid.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a meadow of 12 squares and a 'new herds' circle. Put 3 beans on the meadow.

setup.art: A child's hand adding beans to the grid, one new bean beside each pair of beans already there.
setup.caption: 2. Each year, add 1 fawn for every 2 chital.

setup.art: A hand moving some beans from the grid into the circle, with a die on the table beside the paper.
setup.caption: 3. Send some chital to new herds. Then roll the die for the year.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a sheet of paper. 2. Draw 12 squares in 3 rows of 4, and a circle beside them. 3. Copy the year card where everyone can see it. 4. Put 3 beans on each meadow.
flow.say: Each bean is a chital on your meadow. The meadow grows enough grass for 12. Your job is to send out as many chital as you can in ten years.
flow.kid: Draw 12 squares and a circle. Copy the year card. Put 3 beans on your meadow.
flow.parent: Rajma, chana or small buttons all work as chital. Each player needs about 30.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Meadow Game. Here you draw the meadow and place the first three chital.

flow.do: 1. Play one year together as practice. 2. Add the fawns. 3. Ask each player how many chital they will send away, and why. 4. Roll the die and read the year card.
flow.say: Before you roll, decide how many to send away. A big herd has more fawns. But a herd that is too big has trouble.
flow.kid: Add 1 fawn for every 2 chital. Choose how many to send away. Then roll.

ask.q: What could go wrong for a herd of 12?
good: A drought year feeds only 6, so 6 die and 2 more.
Disease takes half of a herd of 9 or more.
The fawns born next year will be too many for the grass.

flow.parent: Let each player choose freely. Some will keep every chital, and some will send them all away. Both choices teach something by year four.
flow.context: This is the practice year of the Meadow Game. Here you learn the three parts of a turn.

flow.do: 1. Play ten years. 2. Each year, write the numbers in the score table. 3. After year five, stop and ask who is ahead, and what size of herd they keep.
flow.say: We are half way. Look at the tables. Who has sent out the most? How big a herd do they keep on the meadow?
flow.kid: Play ten years. Fill in your table each year. At year five, see who is ahead.

check.q: A herd of 12 has 6 fawns. The meadow feeds 12. What must the player do to lose none?
check.why: The meadow feeds 12, so at least 6 must leave. If all 18 stay, 6 die for want of grass and 2 more die with them. Choosing 'keep all 18' means thinking of the meadow as endless.

flow.parent: Players who keep 6 to 8 chital usually do best. A herd of 12 is hit by drought, by disease and by its own fawns. A herd of 2 has almost no fawns.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Meadow Game. Here you play ten years and keep a table of your herd.

flow.do: 1. Add up each player's circle and meadow. 2. Compare the tables. 3. Ask what size of herd sent out the most chital. 4. Ask why a full meadow did not do best.
flow.say: Whose herd sent out the most? Was it the biggest herd, the smallest, or one in between?
flow.kid: Add up the beans in your circle and on your meadow. Which herd size sent out the most?

ask.q: Why did a herd kept near the middle send out the most chital?
good: It had enough parents for many fawns.
It still had spare grass, so a drought or a few extra fawns did not kill any.
It was under 9, so disease did not halve it.

flow.think: A fishing village wants the biggest catch every year, for ever. How full should they keep the sea?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Meadow Game. Here you compare scores and work out which herd size did best.

games.title: Which Curve?
games.context: This is a card game about the four shapes of population graph. Each card tells what happened to one population. You point to the curve that fits, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 16 story cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: One bacterium lands in a pot of warm milk. For the first hours she and her daughters double every half hour.
items.b: The J. Nothing is holding them back yet, so they multiply.

items.f: Yeast are put in a tube of sugar water. They multiply, then slow down, and the number stays level.
items.b: The S. The yeast grow up to what the tube can carry and level off.

items.f: Reindeer are put on an island with no predators. They become thousands, eat the lichen bare, and nearly all die in one winter.
items.b: The overshoot and crash. They went past the limit and the food was gone.

items.f: Hares in a northern forest become very many about every ten years, and very few in between.
items.b: The wave. The rise and fall repeats again and again.

items.f: Duckweed is put in a bucket. The small green plants spread until they cover the water, and then the cover stays the same.
items.b: The S. The surface of the water is the limit.

items.f: A few water hyacinth plants reach a lake. For the first months the patch doubles every few weeks.
items.b: The J. There is still plenty of open water, so nothing slows them.

items.f: Rats multiply when the bamboo fruits. When the fruit is finished they eat the rice crop, and then most of them starve.
items.b: The overshoot and crash. The extra food ended, and the rats were far too many.

items.f: Ladybirds and the aphids they eat on a rose hedge. Each becomes many and then few, summer after summer.
items.b: The wave. Predator and prey rise and fall one after the other.

items.f: Rhinos are protected in a park. They grow from a dozen to over two thousand in a century, and now the count rises only a little.
items.b: The S. Growth is slowing as the park fills.

items.f: Mosquitoes in the first weeks of the monsoon, when every tin and tyre holds water.
items.b: The J. There are far more breeding places than mosquitoes.

items.f: Algae in a pond after fertiliser washes in. The water turns thick green, the algae use up what they need, and they die and rot.
items.b: The overshoot and crash. The sudden food let them go far past the limit.

items.f: Lynx, the wild cats who hunt hares, in a northern forest over fifty years.
items.b: The wave. Their number follows the hares up and down, a little later.

items.f: Barnacles settle on a bare rock in the sea. They cover it until no space is left, and the number stays there.
items.b: The S. Space on the rock is the limit.

items.f: The number of people in the world from the year 1800 to the year 2000.
items.b: The J. The number grew faster and faster through those 200 years.

items.f: Locusts after good rain in the desert. They breed into huge swarms, eat everything green, and the swarms die away.
items.b: The overshoot and crash. They used up the food that the rain had grown.

items.f: Field rats and rat snakes in a paddy village, counted for twenty years.
items.b: The wave. More rats feed more snakes, and more snakes mean fewer rats.

printables.title: 4 curve cards to draw: the J, the S, the overshoot and crash, and the wave
items: The J: a line that bends upward more and more steeply
The S: a line that rises, then flattens under a limit
The overshoot and crash: a line that climbs past a limit, then falls almost to zero
The wave: a line that goes up and down again and again

rules: Draw the four curves on four pieces of paper, one on each. Lay them in a row on the table.
Shuffle the 16 story cards and put them in a pile, story side up.
One player reads the top card aloud. On the count of three, everyone puts a finger on the curve they think fits.
Turn the card over and read the answer. Each player who chose that curve wins a bean.
A player who can say what set the limit, or what caused the fall, wins a second bean.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most beans wins. If you play alone, 24 beans or more is a strong score.

setup.art: Four pieces of paper in a row on a table, each with one simple graph line: a J shape, an S shape, a peak that falls to zero, and a row of waves.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the four curves on four papers. Lay them in a row.

setup.art: A child reading a small card aloud while two others each hold a finger ready above the four curve papers.
setup.caption: 2. Read a story card. Everyone points to the curve that fits.

setup.art: A story card turned over to show its answer, and a small heap of beans beside one player.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card to check. A right answer wins a bean.

flow.do: 1. Draw one curve on each of four pieces of paper: a J, an S, an overshoot and crash, and a rise and fall. A quick sketch is fine. 2. Lay them in a row. 3. Cut out the 16 story cards and shuffle them.
flow.say: Here are four shapes that a population's graph can take. Each card tells a true kind of story. We will match the story to its shape.
flow.kid: Draw the four curves. Lay them in a row. Shuffle the story cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Curve? Here you draw the four curves and get the cards ready.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone points to a curve. 4. Turn the card and read the answer. 5. Ask what set the limit or caused the fall.
flow.say: Ask yourself two things. Did the number stop rising? And if it fell, did it rise again?
flow.kid: Read the card. Count to three, then point to the curve that fits.

ask.q: How do you tell an S from an overshoot and crash?
good: In the S, the number levels off and stays.
In the overshoot, the number goes past the limit and then falls fast, because the food was used up.

flow.parent: The J cards are all populations that are still far below their limit. If your child asks 'but what happens next?', that is the right question. Every J becomes one of the other three in the end.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Curve? Here you match each story to one of the four curves.

flow.do: 1. Count the beans. 2. Lay the four J cards together. 3. Ask what each of these populations will do later, and why.
flow.say: These four are all J curves. Can a J go on for ever? What do you think each one turns into later? Why?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Then lay the four J cards together.

check.q: A population is growing on a J-shaped curve. What must happen in the end?
options: It slows, levels off or crashes
It stays the same from now on
check.why: No place has endless food and room. So every J either bends into an S, or overshoots and crashes, or begins to rise and fall. Choosing 'for ever' forgets the limiting factors.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Curve? Here you ask what happens to a J-shaped curve in the end.

experiments.title: The Full Island Test: does a forest keep doubling for ever?
experiments.context: In this experiment a paper grid of 36 squares is an island, and each bean is a tree. In every round each tree drops one seed on a square chosen by dice. You count the trees round by round. You will find out whether a forest can keep doubling on a small island.
experiments.question: If every tree drops one seed in every round, does the forest keep doubling? And what happens to the forest if the island is half the size?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You start with 2 trees and play 9 rounds. Will you end with about 18 trees, about 36, or more than 1,000? In which rounds will the forest add the most trees: the first rounds, the middle rounds or the last? Write both guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same rule in every round: one roll of the dice for each tree that stood at the start of the round. In part 2, change only the size of the island. Start with 2 trees both times. Dice are chance, so no two games are the same. The shape of the graph is what you compare, not the exact numbers.
results_table: Seeds that found an empty square

materials.item: a sheet of plain A4 paper
a ruler and a pencil
dice, of two colours if you have them (one die rolled twice also works)
rajma, chana or small buttons for the trees
squared or graph paper for the line graph
colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw the island. Grow the forest for 9 rounds and draw its graph. Then grow it again on half the island and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every round of both parts. Draw both forests on one line graph, in two colours. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: trees on the full island of 36 squares
example_chart.y: Trees at the end of the round
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different, because dice are chance.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a grid of 6 by 6 squares, the columns numbered 1 to 6 along the top and the rows numbered 1 to 6 down the side, with two beans on two of the squares.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 36 squares. Number the columns and the rows 1 to 6. Put 2 beans on any 2 squares.

setup.art: A child rolling two dice of different colours beside the grid, with a finger on the square where the column and the row meet.
setup.caption: 2. For each tree, roll the dice. One die gives the column and the other gives the row.

setup.art: The grid with about twenty beans on it, a new bean being placed on an empty square, and a notebook table beside it.
setup.caption: 3. An empty square gets a new tree. A square with a tree already gets nothing. Count the trees after every round.

flow.do: 1. Draw a square 18 centimetres wide on the paper. 2. Divide it into 6 columns and 6 rows, each 3 centimetres wide. 3. Number the columns 1 to 6 along the top and the rows 1 to 6 down the side. 4. Put a bean on any two squares. 5. Draw the results table with columns for the round, trees at the start, seeds that died and trees at the end.
flow.say: This grid is an island with room for 36 trees, one on each square. Two trees have arrived. Let's draw the table before we start.
flow.kid: Draw 6 columns and 6 rows. Number them 1 to 6. Put a bean on any two squares. Draw the table.
flow.parent: If you have one die, roll it twice: the first roll is the column and the second is the row. Decide which die is 'column' before you start, and keep to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Full Island Test. Here you draw an island of 36 squares and place the first two trees.

flow.do: 1. Explain the rule: each tree drops one seed in every round. 2. Ask for the first guess and its reason. 3. Ask for the second guess and its reason. 4. Write both down.
flow.say: Two trees, and each drops a seed every round, for 9 rounds. How many trees will there be at the end? In which rounds will the forest grow fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many trees you will have after 9 rounds. Guess which rounds add the most. Write both guesses down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: It doubles each round, so it gets huge.
There are only 36 squares, so it cannot pass 36.
It grows fastest at the end, because there are the most trees then.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say the forest will keep doubling, or that it will grow fastest at the end. The dice will answer.
flow.context: This step of the Full Island Test is for guessing. You guess before you roll any dice.

flow.do: 1. Count the trees and write the number under 'Trees at the start'. 2. Roll the two dice once for each of those trees: one die gives the column and the other gives the row. 3. If the square is empty, put a new bean there. 4. If the square has a bean, the seed dies: make a tally mark. 5. Play rounds 1 to 3 this way.
flow.say: Roll once for each tree that was here when the round began. A seed needs light. A seed that lands under a grown tree gets too little light and dies.
flow.kid: Count the trees. Roll once for each one. Empty square: add a bean. Full square: the seed dies. Play 3 rounds.
flow.parent: A seed that lands on a square filled earlier in the same round also dies. In these first rounds almost every seed lives, so the forest nearly doubles.
flow.context: This is the first playing step of the Full Island Test. Here you play three rounds and learn the rule.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 4 to 9 in the same way. 2. One person rolls and calls the square. The other places the bean and keeps the tally. 3. Fill in the table after each round. 4. Stop early only if all 36 squares are full.
flow.say: Keep going to round 9. Watch the tally of seeds that died. What is happening to it, round by round?
flow.kid: Play rounds 4 to 9. Fill in the table each round. Watch how many seeds die.

check.q: The island has 30 trees. Why do most seeds die in this round?
options: The trees are too old to make good seeds
Most squares already have a tree
Seeds die when there are many seeds
check.why: With 30 trees, only 6 squares in 36 are empty, so most seeds land under a tree. The trees and seeds are the same as before. Choosing 'old trees' or 'unlucky dice' looks for a change in the trees or the dice, but only the room has changed.

flow.parent: These rounds have the most rolls, about 30 each near the end. Working as a pair keeps it quick. Late rounds add only one or two trees, and some add none. That slow end is the finding.
flow.context: This is the long step of the Full Island Test. Here you play rounds 4 to 9 and watch what happens as the island fills.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, mark rounds 0 to 9 along the bottom. 2. Mark trees from 0 to 40 up the side. 3. Plot the trees at the end of each round and join the points. 4. In the table, find the round that added the most trees.
flow.say: Now let's turn the table into a picture. Look at the table first. How many trees did the forest add in each round?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Rounds go along the bottom, trees up the side.

ask.q: What shape is the line?
good: It starts slowly, gets steep in the middle and goes flat at the top, like an S.

ask.q: When did the forest add the most trees?
good: In the middle rounds, when it had about 12 to 24 trees.
When about half the squares were full.

flow.parent: The biggest gain usually comes in round 4 or 5, when the island is about half full. Do not explain why yet. Ask your child what they notice about that round.
flow.context: This step of the Full Island Test turns your table into a line graph. Here you also find the round with the biggest gain.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper so that only rows 1 to 3 show. 2. Change the row rule: a roll of 1 or 2 means row 1, 3 or 4 means row 2, and 5 or 6 means row 3. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Start with 2 trees and play 8 rounds. 5. Plot this forest on the same graph in another colour.
flow.say: Half the island has gone under the sea. The trees are the same and the rule is the same. Where will this forest stop? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fold the island in half. Play 8 rounds. Plot this forest in a new colour.
flow.parent: This part is quick, about 85 rolls in all. The forest levels off at or just under 18 trees.
flow.context: This is part 2 of the Full Island Test. Here you grow the same forest on an island of only 18 squares.

flow.do: 1. Lay the graph and the table side by side. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Your child writes the three sentences. 4. Only then share the note below.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? And why did the forest stop where it did?
flow.kid: Answer the three questions out loud. Then write your three sentences.

ask.q: Each tree did the same thing in every round. So why did the forest stop growing?
good: The island ran out of empty squares.
More and more seeds landed under trees and died.
The number of squares set the limit, not the trees.

ask.q: Why did the half island stop near 18?
good: It had only 18 squares.
The limit comes from the size of the place.

flow.parent: After your child has spoken: the forest stopped at the number of squares. Scientists call that number the carrying capacity of the island. The forest grew fastest in the middle because there were many parent trees and still many empty squares.
flow.context: This step of the Full Island Test is for explaining. Here you say what you thought, what you saw and why.

flow.do: 1. Ask what one change would raise the limit of the paper island. 2. Ask what one change would lower it. 3. If there is time, test one idea for 5 rounds.
flow.say: You are in charge of the island now. What one change would let it hold more trees? What change would make it hold fewer? Why?
flow.kid: Pick one change and test it for 5 rounds, if there is time.
flow.think: Real trees die of age and storms. If two trees fell in every round, would the forest stay at 36?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Full Island Test. Here you think of your own change to the island and what it would do.

experiments.title: The Rats and Snakes Game: what happens to hunters and hunted over many rounds?
experiments.context: In this experiment beans are field rats and cardboard squares are rat snakes. You scatter the rats on a cloth and toss the snakes onto them. Rats who are touched are eaten. You count both for 14 rounds and draw two lines on one graph. You will find out which number peaks first, and why.
experiments.question: When snakes eat rats and both have young, what happens to the two numbers over 14 rounds?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Say what you think the rat numbers and the snake numbers will do over 14 rounds. You can sketch it too. Will the two lines rise together, or one after the other? Which will reach its peak first? Write the reason for your guess.
experiments.fair_test: Keep the same cloth, folded to the same size. Stand at the same place for every toss, and toss each card once. Count carefully and use the same rules in every round. Tosses are chance, so every game is different. This is a model of a field. Real fields also have owls, weather and other food.

materials.item: a hand towel or a piece of cloth, folded to about 40 by 30 centimetres
rajma or other large beans, for the rats
squares of thin cardboard, 10 centimetres wide, cut from cereal or sweet boxes, for the snakes
scissors and a ruler
squared or graph paper
colour pencils

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the cardboard if it is thick. Pick up every bean afterwards, so that small children and pets do not swallow them.

schedule.what: Cut the snake cards. Play 14 rounds of tossing and counting. Draw both lines on one graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 14 rounds. Draw one graph with two lines, rats in one colour and snakes in another. Mark each peak. Then write what you thought, what you saw and why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one game (your numbers will be different)

setup.art: A folded towel on the floor with about a dozen beans scattered over it and one square of cardboard beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a cloth to 40 by 30 centimetres. Scatter 12 beans on it. These are the rats.

setup.art: A child standing one big step back from the cloth, tossing a flat cardboard square toward the beans.
setup.caption: 2. From one big step away, toss each snake card once onto the cloth.

setup.art: A cardboard square lying on the cloth with four beans under its edge, and a hand lifting the square to take those beans away.
setup.caption: 3. Every bean under or touching the card is eaten. Three or more, and the snake lives and has one young.

flow.do: 1. Cut 16 squares of thin cardboard, each 10 centimetres wide. 2. Fold the cloth to about 40 by 30 centimetres and lay it flat on the floor. 3. Count out 80 beans into a bowl. You will only use 12 at the start. 4. Draw the results table with 14 rows and columns for the round, the rats and the snakes.
flow.say: The cloth is a paddy field. The beans are field rats and the cards are rat snakes. Let's get everything ready and draw the table.
flow.kid: Cut 16 cardboard squares. Fold the cloth and lay it flat. Count 80 beans. Draw the table.
flow.parent: Cereal boxes, sweet boxes and old notebook covers all work. The cloth stops the beans from rolling. On a bare floor they scatter too far.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rats and Snakes Game. Here you make the snake cards and lay out the field.

flow.do: 1. Read the rules aloud. 2. Ask your child to tell you what the rat numbers and the snake numbers will do, and why. A quick sketch is fine too. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: A snake must catch 3 rats to live and have a young one. The rats that are left double.
flow.kid: Tell your grown-up what the rats and the snakes will do. You can sketch it too.

ask.q: Which will peak first, and why?
good: The rats, because the snakes need many rats before they can multiply.
They rise together.
The snakes will eat all the rats.

flow.parent: Any drawing is fine. Many children draw two lines rising together, or the rats falling to zero.
flow.context: This step of the Rats and Snakes Game is for guessing. You draw the two lines you expect before you play.

flow.do: 1. Scatter 12 beans over the cloth from a hand's height. 2. Stand one big step away and toss 1 snake card flat onto the cloth. 3. Take away every bean under or touching the card, then take the card. 4. Three or more beans: the snake lives and has one young. Fewer: the snake dies. 5. Double the beans left on the cloth, up to 80. 6. Write the new numbers and play rounds 2 to 4.
flow.say: Every rat the card touches is eaten. A snake who eats 3 or more lives and has one young. A snake who eats fewer starves. The rats left over each have one young.
flow.kid: Scatter the rats. Toss the snake card. Take away the rats under it. Three or more: the snake lives and has a young one. Double the rats left.
flow.parent: If a card lands off the cloth, toss it again. If no snakes are left, add one, as if a snake came from the next field. If no rats are left, add 4. The field feeds 80 rats at most, so never put down more than 80.
flow.context: This is the first playing step of the Rats and Snakes Game. Here you play four rounds and learn the rules.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds 5 to 14. 2. Scatter the rats afresh at the start of each round. 3. Toss every snake card once, and clear the eaten rats after each toss. 4. Never use more than 16 snakes. 5. Fill in the table each round.
flow.say: Now there are many rats. Watch what happens to the snakes over the next rounds. Then watch what happens to the rats.
flow.kid: Play rounds 5 to 14. Scatter the rats each round. Toss every snake once. Fill in the table.

check.q: The field has 14 snakes and only 30 rats. What will most likely happen to the snakes next?
options: Many catch fewer than 3 and die
check.why: With 30 rats spread over the field, most cards touch only one or two. Those snakes starve. Choosing 'they double' forgets that the snakes' number depends on the rats' number.

flow.parent: In most games the rats fill the field by round 5 or 6. The snakes peak two or three rounds later, then the rats fall, and then the snakes fall. In some games the snakes stay few for a long time. Play on and see.
flow.context: This is the long step of the Rats and Snakes Game. Here you play ten more rounds and watch both numbers change.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, mark rounds 1 to 14 along the bottom. 2. Mark 0 to 80 up the side. 3. Plot the rats in one colour and join the points. 4. Plot the snakes in another colour. 5. Circle the highest point of each line.
flow.say: Let's draw both lines on one graph. Circle the highest point of each line.
flow.kid: Draw both lines on one graph. Circle the top of each line.

ask.q: How many rounds after the rats' peak did the snakes peak?
good: About one to three rounds later.

flow.parent: The snake line is low, so it can look flat. If it does, draw the snakes again on their own graph with 0 to 16 up the side.
flow.context: This step of the Rats and Snakes Game turns your table into a graph with two lines.

flow.do: 1. Put the written guess beside the real graph. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. 3. Your child writes the three sentences. 4. Only then share the note below.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? And why did the snakes' peak come after the rats' peak?
flow.kid: Answer the three questions out loud. Then write your three sentences.

ask.q: Why did the snakes rise only after the rats?
good: A snake needs plenty of rats near her before she can catch 3.
Snakes multiply only when the rats are already many.

ask.q: Why did the rats fall?
good: There were so many snakes that they ate rats faster than the rats could double.

flow.parent: After your child has spoken: predators can multiply only after their prey is plentiful, and they starve only after the prey has fallen. That delay keeps both numbers swinging. One game shows about one and a half waves.
flow.think: What if the rats had a burrow where five of them were always safe? Would the waves be bigger or smaller?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Rats and Snakes Game. Here you compare your guess with your graph and explain the delay.

activities.title: Doubling Rice: on which square does the rice run out?
activities.context: In this activity you put rice grains on a grid of squares. Each square gets double the grains of the square before. You find out how fast doubling grows, and what stops it.

materials.item: a sheet of plain A4 paper
a ruler and a pencil
raw rice
a plate, to tip the rice back into the jar afterwards

activities.record: Under your grid, write the number of grains for squares 1 to 17. Circle the first square that needs more than a one-kilogram packet.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a grid of 16 squares in 4 rows of 4, with one grain of rice on the first square, two on the second and four on the third.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 16 squares. Put 1 grain on the first, 2 on the second and 4 on the third.

setup.art: The same grid with the eighth square crowded with rice grains and a child counting grains in tens beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Keep doubling up to square 8. Watch how full the squares become.

setup.art: A notebook page with a column of doubling numbers from 1 to 65,536 and one number circled.
setup.caption: 3. Go on doubling on paper up to square 17. Find where a whole packet runs out.

flow.do: 1. Draw 16 squares on the paper, in 4 rows of 4. Make each square 5 centimetres wide. 2. Number them 1 to 16. 3. Ask which square will be the first too small for its rice, and write down the guess.
flow.say: Square 1 gets one grain. Each next square gets double. Which square will be the first that the grains do not fit on, in one flat layer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw 16 squares and number them. Then make your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Doubling Rice. Here you draw the grid and guess where the rice stops fitting.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 grain on square 1, 2 on square 2 and 4 on square 3. 2. Keep doubling: 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. 3. Count the big squares in heaps of ten. 4. Try to fit 256 grains flat on square 9.
flow.say: Keep doubling. What do you notice about the first few squares? What do you notice now?
flow.kid: Put 1, 2, 4, 8 grains. Keep doubling up to square 8. Then try to fit 256 on square 9.

ask.q: What do you notice?
good: It starts very slowly.
Each square has more than all the squares before it put together.
Square 9 will not fit in one layer.

flow.parent: Squares 1 to 8 need 255 grains in all. The 256 grains for square 9 cannot lie in one layer on a 5 centimetre square. With long-grain rice, even the 128 of square 8 may not.
flow.context: This is the counting step of Doubling Rice. Here you put real grains on the squares, doubling each time.

flow.do: 1. On paper, go on doubling from square 9 to square 17. 2. A one-kilogram packet holds roughly 50,000 grains. 3. Find the first square that needs more than a packet. 4. Tip all the rice back into the jar.
flow.say: The numbers took 8 squares to reach 128. How many more squares do they need to pass 50,000? Work it out, then compare it with your guess from the start.
flow.kid: Double on paper up to square 17. Which square needs more than a packet? Put the rice back.

check.q: Rice doubles on each square. Square 10 has 512 grains. How many grains does square 11 have?
check.why: Doubling means multiplying by 2, and 512 × 2 = 1,024. Choosing 522 or 612 means adding the same amount each time. Doubling adds more at every step.

flow.parent: The numbers are 256, 512, 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, 8,192, 16,384, 32,768 and 65,536. Square 17 is the first to pass 50,000. Ask what ran out first on the table: the rice, or the room on a square.
flow.think: A bacterium can double every 20 minutes. Why has the kitchen not filled up with bacteria?
flow.context: This is the last step of Doubling Rice. Here you carry on the doubling on paper and find where a packet of rice runs out.

activities.title: Count Without Counting: how many beans are in the bowl?
activities.context: In this activity you estimate how many beans are in a bowl without counting them all. You mark 40, mix them back in, and look at what share of a new sample is marked. Scientists estimate wild animals in the same way.

materials.item: pale beans such as lobia or white chana
a large bowl and a small cup
a sketch pen or a marker
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write your first guess, the number marked in each of three samples, your estimate, and the real count. Write one sentence on how close the estimate came.

setup.art: A child marking pale beans with a dot from a sketch pen, with a large bowl of unmarked beans beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Take 40 beans out of the bowl. Mark each one with a dot on both sides.

setup.art: A hand stirring a big bowl of beans in which a few dotted beans can be seen among many plain ones.
setup.caption: 2. Put the marked beans back and mix very well.

setup.art: A small cup of beans tipped out on a plate, with the few dotted beans pushed to one side and counted.
setup.caption: 3. Take 40 beans without looking. Count how many are marked.
