flow.do: 1. Pour 3 or 4 big handfuls of beans into the bowl. Do not count them. 2. Ask your child to guess the number by looking, and write it down. 3. Ask how they could find out without counting every bean.
flow.say: How many beans are in this bowl? Guess by looking. Now, how could we find out without counting them all? What is your idea?
flow.kid: Write down your guess. Then think of a way to find out without counting all the beans.
flow.parent: Any idea is welcome: weighing a few, counting one cupful, measuring the depth. Each is a kind of sampling.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count Without Counting. Here you guess the number of beans in a bowl by eye.

flow.do: 1. Take out 40 beans. 2. Mark each one with a dot on both sides. 3. Let the ink dry for a minute. 4. Put them back and stir the bowl 20 times.
flow.say: We have caught 40 beans and marked them. Now they go back and mix with all the others. Stir well, so the marked ones are spread through the whole bowl.
flow.kid: Take out 40 beans. Put a dot on both sides of each. Put them back. Stir 20 times.
flow.context: This is the marking step of Count Without Counting. Here you mark 40 beans and mix them back into the bowl.

flow.do: 1. With eyes closed, scoop beans out with the cup until you have 40. 2. Count how many of the 40 are marked. 3. Put them all back, stir, and do this twice more. 4. Add the three counts and divide by 3. This is the average, also called the mean. 5. Divide 1,600 (that is 40 × 40) by the average.
flow.say: If 8 of your 40 are marked, that is one fifth. So our 40 marked beans are about one fifth of the bowl. What does that make the whole bowl?
flow.kid: Scoop 40 beans with eyes closed. Count the marked ones. Do it three times. Find the average of your three counts. Divide 1,600 by it.

ask.q: Why do we divide 1,600 by the number marked?
good: The share of marked beans in the sample should match the share in the bowl.
40 marked out of the whole bowl is the same share as the marked ones out of 40, and 40 × 40 = 1,600.

flow.parent: With about 200 beans, expect 6 to 10 marked in each sample. Three samples are used because one sample can be a fluke. If a sample has no marked beans at all, stir more and take it again.
flow.context: This is the sampling step of Count Without Counting. Here you take three samples and work out an estimate.

flow.do: 1. Now count every bean in the bowl, in heaps of ten. 2. Compare the real number with the estimate and with the first guess. 3. Ask why the estimate was not exact. 4. Ask how this could work for tigers.
flow.say: Now we count them all, to check. How close was the estimate? How close was your first guess? Why was the estimate not exactly right?
flow.kid: Count all the beans in tens. Compare the real number with your estimate and your first guess.

check.q: You marked 40 beans. A new sample of 40 has 10 marked. About how many beans are in the bowl?
check.why: 10 out of 40 is one quarter. So the 40 marked beans are about one quarter of the bowl, and 40 × 4 = 160. Choosing 400 multiplies 40 by 10, which mixes up the share with the count.

flow.parent: An estimate within about a quarter of the real number is a good result. For tigers, the stripes are the marks. A camera photo is a capture, and a second photo of the same tiger is a recapture.
flow.think: What would go wrong with the estimate if the marked beans were stickier and clumped together?
flow.context: This is the last step of Count Without Counting. Here you count every bean to check your estimate.

activities.title: The Island Graph: plot the reindeer of St Matthew Island
activities.context: In this activity you plot four real counts of reindeer on St Matthew Island, off Alaska. In 1944 people put 29 reindeer there. The island had plenty of lichen to eat and no predators. You guess the end of the graph before you draw it. You will find out what happens when a herd has everything it needs.

materials.item: a sheet of squared or graph paper
a ruler and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the graph. Under it write the shape of the curve, and one sentence on why the number fell.

example_chart.title: The real counts of reindeer on St Matthew Island

setup.art: A sheet of graph paper with the years 1944 to 1966 along the bottom and numbers from 0 to 6,000 up the side, with three points plotted and joined.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the axes. Plot the counts for 1944, 1957 and 1963.

setup.art: The same graph with a dotted pencil line continuing upward as a guess, and a fourth point near zero plotted in 1966.
setup.caption: 2. Guess where the line goes next. Then plot the real count for 1966.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line along the bottom and mark every second year from 1944 to 1966. 2. Draw a line up the side and mark 0 to 6,000 in thousands. 3. Plot 29 in 1944, 1,350 in 1957 and 6,000 in 1963. 4. Join the three points.
flow.say: Twenty-nine reindeer were left on an island with thick lichen and no wolves. Here are the first three counts. Let's plot them.
flow.kid: Draw the axes. Plot 29, then 1,350, then 6,000. Join the points.
flow.parent: Do not show the 1966 count yet. Cover the last row of the table with your thumb.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Island Graph. Here you plot the first three counts of reindeer.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw a dotted line for where the graph goes after 1963, or to say a number for 1966. 2. Ask for the reason. 3. Write the guess beside the graph.
flow.say: The island is small, and lichen grows back very slowly. What do you think the count was three years later, in 1966? Draw your guess, or just say a number.
flow.kid: Draw a dotted line after 1963, or say a number for 1966.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: It keeps going up, because it was going up fast.
It levels off, because the island fills up.
It falls, because they eat all the food.

flow.parent: All three guesses are reasonable. A levelling-off is what the Full Island Test would predict.
flow.context: This step of the Island Graph is for guessing. You guess the 1966 count before you see it.

flow.do: 1. Show the 1966 count: 42. 2. Plot it and join the line. 3. Ask what could explain the fall. 4. Ask how this differs from the Full Island Test.
flow.say: In 1966 a scientist found 42 reindeer and many skeletons. What do you think happened?
flow.kid: Plot 42 for 1966. Join the line.

check.q: A herd grows far past what its island can feed. What usually follows?
options: The herd stays at the high number
Most of the herd dies in a short time
check.why: A herd above the limit eats the food faster than it grows back. When the food is gone, most starve. Choosing 'stays high' treats the food as endless.

ask.q: Why did the reindeer not level off like the paper forest?
good: A seed dies at once if there is no room, so the forest gets the message straight away.
The reindeer could live on lichen that had built up over many years, so they went past the limit before they felt it.

flow.parent: Scientists agree on the counts. They still argue about how much was hunger and how much was one terrible winter. The herd had also eaten most of the lichen. The last reindeer died out by the 1980s.
flow.think: Is there anything people are using up faster than it grows back?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Island Graph. Here you plot the real 1966 count and explain the fall.

activities.title: Limit Detective: what holds the number down?
activities.context: In this activity you choose three living beings you can see from your window or street. For each one you work out the limiting factor: the one need that is in shortest supply for them.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a window, a balcony or a doorstep

activities.record: Make a table with a row for each being: what they eat, where they breed or nest, who eats them, and the limiting factor you chose. Add one way you could test your idea.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook, looking out at crows on a wire, a street dog and a pigeon on a ledge.
setup.caption: 1. Choose three living beings you can see from home.

setup.art: A notebook table with the columns food, breeding place, enemies and limit, and one row filled in for 'house crow'.
setup.caption: 2. For each one, find what they need. Circle the need in shortest supply.

flow.do: 1. Go to a window, balcony or doorstep. 2. Choose three beings you can see or often see. 3. Good choices are a house crow, a pigeon, a street dog, a squirrel, ants, mosquitoes or a weed in a crack. 4. Draw a table with a row for each being. Add columns for what they eat, where they breed or nest, who eats them, and the limiting factor.
flow.say: Pick three living beings who live near us. For each one, ask a detective's question. Why are there not ten times as many of them here?
flow.kid: Choose three living beings near home. Draw a table with a row for each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Limit Detective. Here you choose three living beings near your home.

flow.do: 1. For each being, fill in what they eat and where the food comes from. 2. Fill in where they nest or breed. 3. Fill in who eats them or what kills them. 4. Circle the one need that looks hardest to get.
flow.say: What do they eat here? Where do they raise their young? What kills them? Now, which of these is hardest for them to get on our street? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill in food, breeding place and enemies. Circle the need that is hardest to get.

ask.q: What limits the pigeons here?
good: Food, because they gather where people scatter grain.
Ledges to nest on.

ask.q: What limits the mosquitoes?
good: Still water to lay eggs in.
In the dry months there are few of them.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer. A good answer names one need and gives a reason from what your child has seen. For street dogs and crows, the usual limit is food from rubbish.
flow.context: This is the main step of Limit Detective. Here you find the limiting factor for each being.

flow.do: 1. For one being, ask how the number would change if the limiting factor doubled. 2. Ask how you could test the idea without harming anyone. 3. Write the test in the notebook.
flow.say: Suppose the limiting thing doubled. What would happen to their number? How could we check your idea just by watching and counting?
flow.kid: Pick one being. Think of a test you could do by watching and counting.

check.q: A street has plenty of food for crows but only two tall trees. What most likely limits the crows who nest there?
check.why: Growth stops at the first need that runs short. Food is plentiful, so the scarce thing is places to nest. Choosing 'food' names the need we think of first, not the one in short supply.

flow.think: What is the limiting factor for the plants in a pot on your balcony?
flow.context: This is the last step of Limit Detective. Here you plan a way to test one of your ideas.

activities.title: How Many Tigers Can a Forest Feed?
activities.context: In this activity you work out how many tigers a forest can hold from the number of deer and other large prey in it. You use two numbers from real studies of tigers in India.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
small beans or buttons

activities.record: Write the sum for each forest, and one sentence on what a forest needs before it can hold more tigers.

setup.art: A notebook page with a drawing of a forest holding many small deer and one tiger, and the number 50 written beside the tiger.
setup.caption: 1. One tiger eats about 50 large prey animals in a year.

setup.art: Ten beans in a row with one bean pushed aside, labelled 'tigers take about 1 in 10'.
setup.caption: 2. Tigers can take only about 1 in every 10 prey each year. Work out the prey one tiger needs.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that a forest holds 1,000 deer, pigs and gaur. A gaur is a huge wild ox. 2. Ask how many tigers can live there, and why. 3. Write the guess.
flow.say: A forest has 1,000 large prey animals. One tiger eats about 50 of them a year. How many tigers can live there, year after year? Why?
flow.kid: A forest has 1,000 prey animals. A tiger eats 50 a year. Make your guess and write it down.
flow.parent: Most children divide 1,000 by 50 and say 20. That is a good first step. The next step shows what it leaves out.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Many Tigers Can a Forest Feed? Here you guess the number of tigers for a forest with 1,000 prey.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the forest would look like after one year with 20 tigers. 2. Lay out 10 beans as the prey. 3. Explain that tigers can take only about 1 bean in 10 each year. 4. Work out how many prey one tiger needs, and how many tigers 1,000 prey can feed.
flow.say: If 20 tigers ate all 1,000 this year, what would they eat next year? The prey must have young, and leopards, wild dogs and illness take some too. Tigers can take about 1 in 10.
flow.kid: Twenty tigers would eat all 1,000 prey in one year. Tigers can safely take only 1 in 10. Work out the real number.

ask.q: How many prey animals must a forest hold for one tiger?
good: About 500, because 50 is one tenth of 500.

ask.q: So how many tigers for 1,000 prey?
good: About 2.

flow.parent: The 50 and the 1 in 10 come from a study of 11 Indian forests by K. Ullas Karanth and others in 2004. Both are averages. The 500 is our own sum from them.
flow.context: This is the working step of How Many Tigers Can a Forest Feed? Here you find how many prey one tiger needs.

flow.do: 1. Give two real forests of 100 square kilometres each. 2. The first has 5 prey animals in each square kilometre. The second has 60. 3. Your child works out the prey and the tigers for each. 4. Ask what a forest needs before it can hold more tigers.
flow.say: Here are two forests of the same size. One has 5 prey animals in each square kilometre and the other has 60. How many tigers can each one feed?
flow.kid: Forest A has 5 prey in each square kilometre. Forest B has 60. Each is 100 square kilometres. Work out the tigers.

check.q: A forest's deer are hunted until few are left. The tigers are not hunted. What happens to the tigers?
check.why: The number of tigers a forest can hold depends on its prey. With few deer, tigers have fewer cubs that live, and some leave or starve. Choosing 'stays the same' treats the tigers' number as if it belonged to the tigers alone.

flow.parent: Forest A: 500 prey, so about 1 tiger. Forest B: 6,000 prey, so about 12 tigers. The real study found from 3 to 17 tigers in 100 square kilometres, and more tigers where there were more prey.
flow.context: This is the last step of How Many Tigers Can a Forest Feed? Here you compare a forest with few prey and one with many.

activities.title: The Human Curve: eight billion and slowing
activities.context: In this activity you plot the years in which the number of people in the world passed each billion. You find out whether our own population is still speeding up.

materials.item: a sheet of squared or graph paper
a ruler and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the graph. Write the number of years each billion took, and say whether the growth is speeding up or slowing down.

example_chart.title: When the world's people passed each billion (United Nations estimates)

setup.art: A sheet of graph paper with years from 1800 to 2100 along the bottom and 0 to 11 billion up the side, with eight points rising steeply to the right.
setup.caption: 1. Plot the year for each billion, from 1 to 8.

setup.art: A notebook list of the gaps between the years, with the smallest gap circled.
setup.caption: 2. Work out how many years each billion took. Find the fastest.

flow.do: 1. Mark the years 1800 to 2100 along the bottom, in steps of 25. 2. Mark 0 to 11 billion up the side. 3. Plot the eight points from the table. 4. Join them with a smooth line.
flow.say: This is the population graph of our own species. Plot the eight points.
flow.kid: Mark the years along the bottom. Mark billions up the side. Plot the eight points and join them.

ask.q: What shape is it?
good: A J. It is flat for a long time and then very steep.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Human Curve. Here you plot when the world's people passed each billion.

flow.do: 1. Work out the years between each point and the next. 2. Write them in a row. 3. Ask which billion was added fastest. 4. Ask whether the gaps are still shrinking.
flow.say: How many years did each new billion take? Which one was fastest? Is each billion still coming faster than the one before?
flow.kid: Work out how many years each new billion took.
flow.parent: The gaps are about 123, 33, 14, 13, 12, 12 and 11 years. They stopped shrinking in the 1970s. The United Nations expects the ninth billion to take about 15 years.
flow.context: This is the working step of the Human Curve. Here you find how many years each billion took.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that the United Nations expects a peak of about 10.3 billion in the 2080s. 2. Add that point with a dotted line. 3. Ask what shape the whole curve is becoming. 4. Ask what is slowing it.
flow.say: The United Nations expects about 10.3 billion people in the 2080s, and then a slow fall. Draw that with a dotted line. What shape is the curve becoming? What could be slowing it?
flow.kid: Add 10.3 billion in the 2080s with a dotted line.

check.q: The world's population is still growing, but more slowly. What is the main reason?
options: The Earth has run out of food
People are moving to other countries
check.why: In most countries women now have fewer children than their mothers did. In India the average is about 2. People are living longer, not dying younger. Moving between countries does not change the world's total.

flow.parent: The dotted part is a forecast, not a measurement. The slowing comes mostly from families choosing to have fewer children. That happens where girls stay longer in school and where children survive.
flow.think: A deer herd is slowed by hunger. People are slowing their own number mostly by choice. Is that the same kind of limit?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Human Curve. Here you add the expected peak and look at the shape of the whole curve.

projects.title: Crowded Cups: does sowing more seeds give more methi?
projects.context: In this three-week project you sow 5, 25 and 100 methi seeds in three cups of the same size. Methi is fenugreek. You give each cup the same water and light, and find out what crowding does to living plants.

materials.item: paper cups or steel tumblers of the same size
garden soil or potting soil
materials.qty: enough to fill the 3 cups three-quarters full

materials.item: methi seeds from the kitchen
a tablespoon, a ruler and a marker pen
a bright windowsill or balcony ledge
a kitchen scale, if you have one

projects.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cups. Wash your hands after touching soil. Do not eat seedlings from a cup that has mould.

schedule.what: Fill the cups, sow 5, 25 and 100 seeds, and write your guess.
Count the plants in each cup and measure the five tallest.
Count and measure again. Look at leaf colour and at plants that have fallen over.
Count and measure for the last time. Cut each cup's plants, compare the three harvests, and explain.

projects.record: Make a table with a row for each cup on days 7, 14 and 21: seeds sown, plants alive, height of the five tallest, leaf colour and plants fallen over. On day 21 add the harvest. Write what you thought, what you saw and why.

setup.art: Three paper cups of soil in a row on a windowsill, labelled 5, 25 and 100, with methi seeds lying on the soil: a few in the first cup and a thick layer in the third.
setup.caption: 1. Sow 5, 25 and 100 methi seeds in three cups of the same size.

setup.art: A child's hand pouring one tablespoon of water into each of the three cups in turn.
setup.caption: 2. Give every cup the same water each day and the same light.

setup.art: Three cups of methi seedlings three weeks old: a few sturdy dark green plants in the first, and a crowd of thin, pale, leaning plants in the third.
setup.caption: 3. After 7, 14 and 21 days, count the plants, measure them and compare.

flow.do: 1. Poke three small holes in the bottom of each paper cup and stand the cups on a plate. 2. Fill each cup three-quarters full of soil. 3. Label them 5, 25 and 100. 4. Count out the seeds and spread them evenly on the soil. 5. Cover them with a thin layer of soil and give each cup 2 tablespoons of water. 6. Ask for a guess and write it down.
flow.say: The third cup has 20 times as many seeds as the first. Will it grow 20 times as much methi? What will the plants in each cup look like? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sow 5, 25 and 100 seeds in three cups. Water them.
flow.parent: Steel tumblers have no holes, so give them only 1 tablespoon of water a day. Water all three cups the same, every day or two, so the soil is damp but not soaked.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Crowded Cups. Here you sow three cups with different numbers of seeds and write your guess.

flow.do: 1. Count the plants standing in each cup. 2. Measure the five tallest in each cup, from the soil to the top. 3. Write the numbers in the table. 4. Ask what your child notices.
flow.say: It is day 7. How many seeds came up in each cup? Do the plants in the three cups look the same or different?
flow.kid: Count the plants in each cup. Measure the five tallest. Write it in the table.
flow.wait: Leave the cups for 7 days, watering them the same.
flow.parent: In the first week the cups often look alike. A seedling's first food is stored inside the seed, so crowding hardly matters yet. In the crowded cup some seeds may sit on top of others and never root.
flow.context: This is day 7 of Crowded Cups. Here you count and measure the seedlings for the first time.

flow.do: 1. Count and measure again. 2. Look at the lowest leaves: are they green or yellow? 3. Count the plants that have fallen over. 4. Look for white fuzz, which is mould.
flow.say: It is day 14. The food stored in the seeds is used up. Now each plant must get light, water and soil food for itself. What has changed?
flow.kid: Count and measure again. Check the leaf colour. Count the fallen plants. Look for white fuzz.
flow.wait: Leave the cups for 7 more days, watering them the same.
flow.parent: Crowded seedlings are usually taller, thinner and paler, because they stretch for light and share the soil. Mould in the crowded cup is a result too. Disease spreads fastest where plants touch.
flow.context: This is day 14 of Crowded Cups. Here you look for the first signs of crowding.

flow.do: 1. Count and measure for the last time. 2. Cut each cup's plants at the soil with scissors. 3. Lay the three harvests side by side, or weigh them. 4. Compare the harvest from 100 seeds with the harvest from 5. 5. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: The third cup had 20 times the seeds. Did it give 20 times the harvest? Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why it came out that way.
flow.kid: Cut the plants in each cup. Lay the three harvests side by side.

ask.q: Why did 100 seeds not give 20 times the methi?
good: All three cups had the same soil, water and light.
In the crowded cup each plant got a smaller share, so each stayed thin, and some died.
The cup set the limit, not the number of seeds.

flow.parent: After your child has spoken: the cup can only support so much plant, however many seeds start. This is carrying capacity in a living population. If all three cups still look healthy, the limit has not been reached yet. Keep them for another week.
flow.wait: Leave the cups for 7 more days, watering them the same.
flow.context: This is the last day of Crowded Cups. Here you compare the three harvests and explain the result.

challenges.title: The Fishing Rule: the biggest catch that can go on for ever
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about a village pond that can hold 36 fish. A table tells you how many new fish the pond adds in a year. You look for the fishing rule that catches the most fish over ten years without emptying the pond.
challenges.problem: The pond is full, with 36 fish. Each year the fish breed, and then the village catches some. Find a rule for how many to catch each year. It must give the biggest total catch over 10 years, and the pond must be able to go on giving that catch afterwards.
constraints: Use the growth table to find the new fish each year. Use the row nearest to your number of fish. If two rows are equally near, use the one with fewer fish.
The pond can never hold more than 36 fish.
At the end of year 10, the pond must hold at least as many fish as it did at the end of year 9.
materials: the growth table: a pond of 6 fish adds 5, 12 adds 8, 18 adds 9, 24 adds 8, 30 adds 5, and 36 adds 0
36 beans, if you want to move real 'fish'

example_chart.title: The growth table: new fish added in one year (from the Full Island rule)

general: Catch a small number, such as 3, every year. The pond stays nearly full, so few new fish are added.
Catch whatever was added that year, and keep the pond where it is.
Catch a lot in the first years and less later.
creative: First fish the pond down to 18, where the table adds the most. Then catch 9 every year, which is exactly what is added.
Keep the pond at 21, a little above the middle, and catch 9. A bad year then does less harm.
Close the pond for two years after any year in which the count falls below 12.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own fishing rule in one sentence. Run it for 10 years in a table. What was your total catch? How many fish are left? Could the village use your rule for 100 years?

setup.art: A notebook page with a small table of two columns, 'fish in the pond' and 'new fish this year', beside a drawing of a round village pond with fish in it.
setup.caption: 1. Read the growth table. A full pond adds no fish. A half-full pond adds the most.

setup.art: A child filling in a ten-row table with the columns fish at start, new fish, catch and fish at end.
setup.caption: 2. Choose a fishing rule. Run it for 10 years and add up the catch.

flow.do: 1. Read the growth table together: 6 fish add 5, 12 add 8, 18 add 9, 24 add 8, 30 add 5, and 36 add 0. 2. Ask where it comes from: the Full Island Test, where the forest grew fastest when half full. 3. Ask why a full pond adds no fish. 4. Draw a table with columns for fish at the start, new fish, catch, and fish at the end.
flow.say: Look at the table. A pond of 36 adds nothing, and a pond of 6 adds 5. Where does the pond add the most?
flow.kid: Read the growth table. Find where the pond adds the most fish. Draw your ten-year table.

ask.q: Why does a full pond add no new fish?
good: There is no food or room left for young fish, so they do not survive.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fishing Rule. Here you read the table of how many new fish a pond adds.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to choose a first rule and say why. 2. Run it for 10 years in the table. 3. Add up the total catch. 4. Check the last constraint: at the end of year 10 the pond must hold at least as many fish as at the end of year 9.
flow.say: Choose your first rule. How many will you catch each year? Why that number? Let's run it for ten years and add up the catch.
flow.kid: Choose a rule and say why. Run it for 10 years. Add up your catch.
flow.parent: A common first rule is 'catch 10 every year'. It gives 100 fish in 10 years, which looks best. But the pond shrinks every year, from 36 to 13, so it fails the last constraint. No row of the table adds 10.
flow.context: This is the first try of the Fishing Rule. Here you test one fishing rule for ten years.

flow.do: 1. Try the three usual rules. 2. Try the creative rules. 3. Write each total catch in a list. 4. Find the rule with the biggest total that still passes the last constraint.
flow.say: Now try some other rules and compare the totals. Which rule gives the most fish and still leaves a pond that can go on?
flow.kid: Try other rules. Write each total. Find the best rule that keeps the pond going.

check.q: A pond holds 36 fish when full. At what number does it add the most new fish each year?
options: About 18, when it is half full
It adds the same at any number
check.why: At 18 there are many parents and still plenty of food and room for young. A full pond has no room, and a nearly empty pond has few parents. Choosing 36 mixes up the most fish with the most new fish.

flow.parent: Fish the pond down to 18 in year one, then take 9 a year. That gives 18 + 9 × 9 = 99 fish, and the pond stays at 18 for ever. Catching 3 a year from a nearly full pond gives only 30.
flow.context: This is the comparing step of the Fishing Rule. Here you test several rules and compare their total catches.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes their own rule in one sentence. 2. They run it for 10 years. 3. Ask what would happen in a year when the real pond added fewer fish than the table says.
flow.say: Write your own rule and test it. Then think about this. Real ponds have bad years. What would your rule do in a year when only 5 new fish came?
flow.kid: Write your own rule. Test it for 10 years.
flow.think: Real fishers cannot see how many fish are in the sea. How could they find out?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Fishing Rule. Here you write and test your own rule, and think about a bad year.

challenges.title: Fewer Mosquitoes Without Spray: lower the limit
challenges.context: This is a design challenge for your own home. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water, and the young take about a week or more to become adults. You plan a way to have fewer mosquitoes by taking away their breeding places.
challenges.problem: Make a plan that lowers the number of mosquitoes at your home for a whole month. You may not use any spray, coil or poison. You can only change the place.
constraints: No spray, coil, oil or poison.
The plan must take no more than 10 minutes a week to keep up.
It must not harm other living beings, such as birds who drink from a bowl.
materials: a torch, for looking into drums and corners
a grown-up to check tanks, the roof and the area round the house
general: Once a week, empty and scrub every container that holds still water: plant saucers, buckets, coolers and tins.
Keep water drums and overhead tanks tightly covered.
Throw away or turn over things that catch rain: coconut shells, old tyres, broken pots.
creative: Change a bird bowl's water every three days. The birds still drink, but no mosquito finishes growing in it.
Keep a few guppies in a garden tank or a lotus pot. Guppies eat mosquito larvae, who are the young that live in water.
Make a street map of still water with your neighbours, and share the weekly check among the houses.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own plan. List every place at home where water stands for more than a week. For each one, write what you will do and how often. After two weeks, check again. Which places did you miss?

setup.art: A child with a torch and a notebook looking into a plant saucer full of water on a balcony, with tiny wriggling larvae drawn in the water.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt for every place at home where water stands still.

setup.art: A hand-drawn plan of a flat and its balcony with crosses marked at a plant saucer, a bucket, a cooler and a covered drum.
setup.caption: 2. Write down each place. Write what you will do there, and how often.

flow.do: 1. Ask what mosquitoes need in order to multiply. 2. Explain that the eggs are laid in still water, and that the young live in the water for about a week. 3. Ask which is easier to change: the mosquitoes, or the water.
flow.say: Killing mosquitoes lowers the number for a day or two. Then more grow up. What do they need that we could take away?
flow.kid: Mosquito young grow in still water for about a week. What could we take away?

ask.q: Why does taking away still water last longer than killing mosquitoes?
good: It lowers the carrying capacity, so fewer can grow up at all.
If the water stays, the survivors lay eggs and the number comes back.

flow.context: This is the first step of Fewer Mosquitoes Without Spray. Here you think about what limits the number of mosquitoes.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home with a torch. 2. Look at plant saucers, buckets, drums, coolers, the fridge tray, the roof and the area outside. 3. Write down each place with still water, or take a photo of it. 4. Look in the water for tiny wrigglers.
flow.say: Let's hunt for still water. Check anything that could hold water for a week. If you see tiny wrigglers that jerk when the water is tapped, those are mosquito young.
flow.kid: Walk round with a torch. Find every place with still water. Write each one down or take a photo.
flow.parent: A grown-up checks the roof, overhead tanks and anything outdoors. Common places people miss are the tray behind the fridge, air cooler tanks and the saucers under pots.
flow.context: This is the hunting step of Fewer Mosquitoes Without Spray. Here you find and map the still water at your home.

flow.do: 1. For each marked place, choose an action: empty weekly, cover, turn over or throw away. 2. Write who will do it, and on which day. 3. Check the plan against the three constraints.
flow.say: For each place, what will we do, and how often? Remember, the young take about a week to grow.
flow.kid: Write an action for each place. Write the day and who does it. Check the three rules.

check.q: Mosquito young need about a week in still water. How often should a plant saucer be emptied?
check.why: If the water is thrown out before the young finish growing, none become adults. Once a month gives them time to finish three or four times over.

flow.context: This is the planning step of Fewer Mosquitoes Without Spray. Here you write an action for each place with still water.

flow.do: 1. Put the plan where the family can see it. 2. Do the first round of emptying together. 3. Set a day two weeks from now to check again.
flow.say: Let's do the first round now. In two weeks we will hunt again. What do you expect to find then? Why?
flow.kid: Put up your plan. Empty the water today. Check again in two weeks.
flow.think: Mosquitoes fly in from other houses. What does that tell you about who needs to join the plan?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fewer Mosquitoes Without Spray. Here you start your plan and set a day to check it.

items.p: What is a population?
opts: All living beings in one place
All members of one species in one place
All the animals of one country
items.why: A population is one species, in one place, at one time. Choosing 'all living beings in one place' describes a community, which holds many populations.

items.p: A population's number changes through births, deaths, members arriving and members ____.
items.why: These are the only four ways. Arriving is called immigration and leaving is called emigration.

items.p: In a herd, 30 kids are born, 12 goats die, 2 arrive and 5 leave. By how many does it grow?
items.why: Add what comes in: 30 + 2 = 32. Add what goes out: 12 + 5 = 17. Then 32 − 17 = 15.

items.p: Which list shows growth by doubling?
items.why: In doubling, each number is 2 times the one before. The other lists add the same amount each time, which is much slower.

items.p: True or false: a population can keep doubling for ever if nobody disturbs it.
items.why: False. Doubling soon needs more food and room than any place has. In Doubling Rice, square 17 already needed more than a whole packet.

items.p: What is a limiting factor?
opts: The biggest animal in a place
A scarce need that holds a number down
The number of young in one year
items.why: A limiting factor is whatever runs short first, such as food, water, room or nesting places. It can also be something that removes members, such as a predator.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: the largest number a place can keep alive year after year
growing past what the place can feed
a fast fall, when many die in a short time
a delay between a cause and its effect
a place where prey are safe

items.p: In the Full Island Test, every tree dropped one seed each round. Why did the forest stop growing?
items.a: The island had only 36 squares. As it filled, more seeds landed on squares that already had a tree, and those seeds died. When every square was full, no seed could live.
items.why: A strong answer says that the trees did not change. The room ran out. The number of squares set the limit.

items.p: Draw the graph of a population that grows slowly, then fast, then levels off. Mark the carrying capacity.
items.a: An S-shaped line that flattens at the top, with a dotted line across at the level where it flattens, labelled 'carrying capacity'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows all three parts: the slow start, the steep middle and the flat top. A line that goes straight up, or that keeps bending upward, has no limit in it.
items.art: A blank pair of axes labelled 'time' along the bottom and 'number' up the side.

items.p: Sort each story into the curve it makes.
items.why: In an S, the number levels off and stays. In an overshoot, it passes the limit and falls fast. In a wave, the rise and fall repeat.
items: yeast in a tube that multiply and then stay level
reindeer who eat an island bare and starve
hares who become many about every ten years
duckweed that covers a bucket and stays
rats who multiply on bamboo fruit and then starve
ladybirds and aphids on a hedge, summer after summer

items.p: Rats and rat snakes live in one field. The rats become many. What happens to the snakes next?
opts: They become many, a little later
items.why: With many rats, more snakes catch enough to live and raise young. That takes time, so the snakes rise after the rats. Choosing 'fewer' reads the link backward.

items.p: Put the four steps of one predator and prey wave in order. Start with the prey rising.
items.why: More prey feed more predators. More predators eat the prey down. Fewer prey starve the predators. Then the prey can rise again.

items.p: Why does the predators' peak come after the prey's peak, and not at the same time?
items.a: Predators can multiply only when prey is already plentiful, and raising young takes time. They start to starve only after the prey has already fallen.
items.why: A strong answer names the delay and gives its cause. 'Because they eat them' is true but does not explain why the predators are late.

items.p: You mark 40 beans in a bowl. A new sample of 40 has 8 marked. About how many beans are there?
items.why: 8 out of 40 is one fifth. So the 40 marked beans are about one fifth of the bowl, and 40 × 5 = 200.

items.p: True or false: the carrying capacity of a meadow is the same in a drought year and a wet year.
items.why: False. Less grass grows in a drought, so the meadow can feed fewer animals that year. Carrying capacity moves with the weather and the seasons.

items.p: One bacterium doubles every 20 minutes. How many are there after 2 hours?
items.why: Two hours is 6 lots of 20 minutes. Double 6 times: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.

items.p: On a full island of 36 trees, how many new trees are added in a round?
items.why: Every square has a tree, so every seed lands under a tree and dies. Choosing 36 forgets that seeds need an empty square.

items.p: When did the paper forest add the most trees in one round?
opts: When about half the squares were full
It added the same every round
items.why: In the middle there are many parent trees and still many empty squares. Early on there are few parents. Late on there is little room.

items.p: A limit that presses harder when a population is more crowded is called density-____.
items.why: Density means how crowded the members are. Disease and hunger are density-dependent, because they are worse in a crowd.

items.p: Sort each cause of death by whether crowding makes it worse.
items.why: Disease, hunger and fights grow worse as members crowd together. A storm, a frost or a fire kills a share of the members whether they are few or many.

items.p: Reindeer on St Matthew Island passed the island's limit and then crashed. Why did they not level off gently?
items.a: They lived on lichen that had built up over many years and grows back very slowly. So the herd could keep growing after it passed what the island could renew. When the lichen was gone, the limit hit all at once.
items.why: A strong answer says the limit arrived late, because the food was a store and not a yearly supply. Naming the hard winter as well is a fair point.

items.p: Reindeer on an island fell from 6,000 to 42. How many died or were missing?
items.why: 6,000 − 42 = 5,958. That is more than 99 in every 100.

items.p: In a small glass tube with no hiding places, hunters and prey are kept together. What usually happens?
opts: They rise and fall for ever
The hunters eat all the prey, then starve
items.why: Georgy Gause found this in the 1930s. With nowhere to hide, every prey animal is caught. Lasting waves need refuges, distance or new arrivals.

items.p: Draw two wavy lines on one graph, for rats and for snakes. Show which peaks first.
items.a: Two wave-shaped lines. The rat line is taller. Each snake peak is a little to the right of a rat peak.
items.why: A strong drawing puts every snake peak after a rat peak. Two lines that rise and fall exactly together leave out the time lag.
items.art: A blank pair of axes labelled 'rounds' along the bottom and 'number' up the side.

items.p: Why are tigers told apart by their stripes in camera photographs?
opts: Stripes show how old a tiger is
No two tigers have the same stripes
Stripes show what a tiger eats
items.why: Each tiger's stripe pattern is her own, like a fingerprint. So a photo counts as a capture of one known tiger, with no need to catch or mark her.

items.p: An estimate from mark and recapture is not exact. Give one thing that could make it wrong.
items.a: The marked beans may not have mixed in well. The sample may be too small. Marked members may be easier or harder to catch than the others.
items.why: Any one of these is a strong answer. The method works only if marked and unmarked members are equally likely to be in the second sample.

items.p: A tiger needs about 500 prey animals in her forest. How many tigers can a forest of 3,000 prey feed?
items.why: 3,000 ÷ 500 = 6. The 500 comes from 50 prey eaten a year, when tigers can take about 1 in 10.

items.p: Three of these raise a pond's carrying capacity for fish. Which one lowers it?
items.why: Fish need oxygen dissolved in the water. Rotting sewage uses it up, so fewer fish can live. The other three add food or room.
opts: Sewage that uses up the oxygen

items.p: Three people talk about the mosquitoes in their street.
items.a: A strong answer says that killing lowers the number for a short time, and that the number returns if the breeding places stay. Clearing still water lowers the carrying capacity itself. It can also grant that spraying helps quickly in an outbreak.
items.why: All three have a point. The lasting change comes from lowering what the place can carry.

views.says: Spray them every evening. The more we kill, the fewer there will be.
Empty every tin and saucer each week. If they cannot breed, the number stays low.
Both. Spray when there is fever in the street, and clear the water all year.

items.ask: Whose plan do you agree with most? Use the idea of carrying capacity in your answer. Then say one fair point from another view.

items.p: A village catches fish from a pond. Why is a half-full pond better for the village than a full one?
items.a: A full pond adds almost no new fish, because there is no food or room for young. A half-full pond has many parents and plenty of room, so it adds the most new fish each year to catch.
items.why: A strong answer separates the number of fish from the number of new fish. The catch that can go on comes from the new fish.

worksheets.title: Why the numbers behave as they do (challenge)

items.p: Why do living populations grow by multiplying, and not by adding the same number each year?
items.a: Because the young grow up and have young too. Every new member is also a new parent, so the more there are, the more are added.
items.why: A strong answer says that the number added depends on the number already there.

items.p: Twenty-nine reindeer double every 2 years. How many are there after 10 years?
items.why: Ten years is 5 doublings: 58, 116, 232, 464, 928.

items.p: A plant has plenty of water and light but stays small in poor soil. What does this show?
opts: Growth stops at the scarcest need
items.why: This is the law of the minimum. The need in shortest supply sets the limit, however plentiful the others are.

items.p: True or false: at carrying capacity, no young are born.
items.why: False. Young are still born, but about as many members die as are born, so the number stays level. On the full island every tree still dropped a seed.

items.p: Draw a hill-shaped graph of 'new members added' against 'size of the population'. Mark where the hill is highest.
items.a: A curve that starts at zero, rises to a peak at about half the carrying capacity, and falls back to zero at the carrying capacity.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the peak in the middle and brings the curve down to zero at the limit. A line that keeps rising says a full place adds the most, which is the opposite of what the test showed.
items.art: A blank pair of axes labelled 'size of the population' along the bottom and 'new members added' up the side.

items.p: Scientists gave hares extra food in one area and kept predators out of another. Why did they also do both together?
items.a: To see whether food and predators act separately or together. Doing both raised hare numbers far more than the two effects added up, so the two limits work together.
items.why: A strong answer says that testing one thing at a time cannot show how two causes combine.

items.p: Mites on a tray of oranges rose and fell three times only when the tray was large and patchy. Why?
opts: Some prey were always out of reach
items.why: In a patchy world, prey can settle on oranges the hunters have not found yet. So the prey are never all caught, and both kinds last.

items.p: Put the events on St Matthew Island in order.
a: 29 reindeer are put on the island
The herd reaches about 6,000 and the lichen is eaten down
Nearly all die in one hard winter
items.why: The herd grew fast with no predators, passed what the island could renew, and then crashed.
items: Nearly all die in one hard winter
29 reindeer are put on the island
The herd reaches about 6,000 and the lichen is eaten down

items.p: Many bacteria sense how crowded they are by chemical signals. This is called ____ sensing.
items.why: A quorum is the number of members needed before a group acts. The bacteria act together only when enough of them are near.

items.p: The world's population estimate for 2022 is given as 'about 8 billion', and India's tigers as 'about 3,682'. Why 'about'?
items.a: Both are estimates from samples and counts that cannot reach everyone. The tiger report gives a range from about 3,167 to 3,925 for this reason.
items.why: A strong answer says that an estimate has a range, and that giving the range is more honest than giving one exact number.

items.p: Published estimates of how many people the Earth can carry range from under 1 billion to over 1,000 billion. Why so wide?
opts: Nobody has tried to measure it
It depends on how people choose to live
items.why: Joel Cohen showed this in 1995. The number depends on what people eat, use and throw away, and how they share. Those are choices, not measurements.

items.p: Three thinkers answer the question: must a growing number of people run out of food?
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence such as the S-shaped curve, the reindeer overshoot, or the way people have raised their own carrying capacity with new farming. It grants a fair point to another view.
items.why: This is still argued about. Each view explains part of what has happened since 1798.

views.says: Yes. People multiply, but farmland can only be added to. Hunger will always catch up.
No. Crowded farmers invent better ways to grow food. Need drives new ideas.
New ideas buy time. But soil, water and fuel are finite, and overshoot is possible.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use one thing from this lesson as evidence. Then say what one of the others gets right.

items.p: Carrying capacity rose for people when forests became farms. What happened to the capacity for the forest's animals?
items.a: It fell. The same land, water and sunlight now feed crops for people, so less is left for deer, hornbills and tigers.
items.why: A strong answer sees that one place has one supply. Raising one species' share lowers the share of others.

items.p: Three of these could make waves of predators and prey last. Which one would end them?
items.why: In a small bare cage every prey animal is found and eaten, and then the hunters starve. The other three keep some prey out of reach or bring new ones in.
opts: New animals arriving now and then

items.p: A herd is fed by lorry every dry season and grows to three times the hill's own limit. What is the risk?
opts: The herd forgets how to graze
A crash if the lorries ever stop
items.why: The herd is now above what the hill can carry by itself. It lasts only as long as the outside food comes. The many feet and mouths also wear the hill down.

quiz.p: Which of these is one population?
opts: All the birds in a park
All the house crows of one town
quiz.why: A population is one species in one place. All the birds in a park are many species, so they are many populations.

quiz.p: Births 40, deaths 25, arrivals 5, departures 20. What happens to the population?
quiz.why: In: 40 + 5 = 45. Out: 25 + 20 = 45. The two match, so the number stays the same though the members change.

quiz.p: A water plant doubles its patch every week. It covers half a pond today. When will it cover the whole pond?
opts: In as long as it took so far
quiz.why: One more doubling turns a half into a whole. Choosing 'as long as it took so far' treats doubling like steady adding.

quiz.p: Why can no population keep doubling for ever?
opts: Animals get tired of having young
Something its members need runs short
quiz.why: Each doubling needs twice the food and room. Any place has only so much, so a limiting factor always appears.

quiz.p: A forest stops at 36 trees on an island of 36 squares. The island is halved. Where does it stop now?
quiz.why: The limit comes from the place. Half the squares means room for half the trees. Choosing 36 treats the limit as belonging to the trees.

quiz.p: What is the carrying capacity of a place?
opts: The number born there in a year
The largest number it can keep alive for years
The heaviest animal it can hold
The number of species in it
quiz.why: It is the number the place can go on feeding and housing without being damaged. It can change with seasons and weather.

quiz.p: A line graph rises slowly, then steeply, then goes flat. What does the flat part mean?
opts: The population has reached its carrying capacity
No young are born any more
quiz.why: On the flat part, births and deaths match, so the number stays level. Young are still being born.

quiz.p: A graph climbs far above a limit line and then drops almost to zero. What is this called?
quiz.why: The population went past what the place could renew, the food ran out, and most members died.

quiz.p: In a field, the number of rats peaks in March. When would you expect the rat snakes to peak?
quiz.why: Snakes multiply only after rats are plentiful, and raising young takes time. So their peak comes after the rats' peak.

quiz.p: Why do predators not usually eat every last one of their prey?
opts: They are kind to their prey
Some prey are always hidden or far away
quiz.why: Refuges, distance and new arrivals keep some prey alive. In a small bare space with no hiding places, the prey are all eaten.

quiz.p: How do scientists estimate the tigers of a forest?
opts: They photograph tigers and match their stripes
quiz.why: Each tiger's stripes are her own. Photos from automatic cameras are treated as captures and recaptures, and the number is worked out from them.

quiz.p: Which change would raise a forest's carrying capacity for tigers?
quiz.why: The number of tigers a forest can hold follows its prey. Bringing in more tigers without more prey only means some will starve or leave.

open_questions.q: Why do snowshoe hares rise and fall across much of Canada at nearly the same time?
open_questions.why_open: Predators and food explain one forest. Scientists still test what keeps forests thousands of kilometres apart in step. Weather and travelling predators are two ideas.

open_questions.q: Is there a carrying capacity of the Earth for people, and can it be measured?
open_questions.why_open: Published estimates range from under 1 billion to over 1,000 billion. The answer depends on how people choose to live, which science cannot decide.

open_questions.q: Why do some populations cycle, while most stay near one number?
open_questions.why_open: The equations allow both. For most wild species nobody has counted for long enough to tell which is happening, or why.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living beings sense their own numbers?
open_questions.why_open: Quorum sensing is well shown in bacteria. Whether trees, fungi or herds do something like it is only beginning to be studied.

open_questions.q: Did hunger or weather kill the reindeer of St Matthew Island?
open_questions.why_open: The counts are agreed, but nobody was on the island that winter. Scientists who study the records still weigh the two causes differently.

maths.problem: In Doubling Rice, square 8 has 128 grains. How many grains does square 12 have?
maths.explain: Double four times, once for each square: 256, 512, 1,024, 2,048. So square 12 has 2,048 grains.
maths.context: This is about Doubling Rice, where each square of a grid gets double the grains of the square before.
maths.why_maths: A doubling pattern lets you work out a square you could never fill with real rice.

maths.problem: A paper forest had 2, 4, 7, 12, 19, 26, 31, 34, 35 and 36 trees at the end of rounds 0 to 9. In which round were the most trees added?
maths.explain: Find the gain in each round by subtracting: 2, 3, 5, 7, 7, 5, 3, 1, 1. The biggest gain is 7, from 12 to 19 and from 19 to 26. That is when the island was about half full.
maths.context: This is about the Full Island Test. A forest of beans grows on a grid of 36 squares, and you count the trees after each round.

chart.title: Made-up example: trees on the island of 36 squares

maths.why_maths: The steepest part of a line graph shows when a thing is changing fastest. Subtracting gives the same answer in numbers.

maths.problem: You marked 40 beans. Three samples of 40 had 7, 9 and 8 marked beans. Estimate the number of beans in the bowl.
maths.explain: The mean number marked is (7 + 9 + 8) ÷ 3 = 8. So 8 out of 40, or one fifth, of a sample is marked. The 40 marked beans are then about one fifth of the bowl. 40 × 5 = 200.
maths.context: This is about Count Without Counting. You mark 40 beans, mix them into a bowl, and see what share of a new sample is marked.
maths.why_maths: A share that you can count in a small sample tells you the size of a whole that you cannot count.

maths.problem: A tiger eats about 50 large prey animals a year, and tigers can take about 1 in 10 of the prey. A forest has 4,000 prey animals. How many tigers can it feed?
maths.explain: One tenth of 4,000 is 400 prey a year for tigers. Each tiger needs 50. 400 ÷ 50 = 8.
maths.context: This is about How Many Tigers Can a Forest Feed? You work out the tigers a forest can hold from its deer, pigs and gaur.
maths.why_maths: Two small sums turn a count of deer into the number of tigers, which is much harder to count.

maths.problem: Reindeer on St Matthew Island grew from 29 in 1944 to about 1,350 in 1957. About how many times did the herd double in those 13 years?
maths.answer: Between 5 and 6 times. So the herd doubled about every two and a half years.
maths.explain: Keep doubling 29: 58, 116, 232, 464, 928, 1,856. After 5 doublings there are 928, and after 6 there are 1,856. The real count of 1,350 lies between them. 13 years ÷ 5.5 is about 2.4 years for each doubling.
maths.context: This is about the Island Graph. In 1944 people put 29 reindeer on an island with plenty of food and no predators.
maths.why_maths: Counting doublings tells you how fast a population was really growing, which the raw numbers hide.

maths.problem: A pond adds 9 new fish a year when it holds 18 fish, and 5 a year when it holds 30. A village wants to catch the same number every year for ever. Which pond size lets them catch more, and how many more in 10 years?
maths.answer: The pond kept at 18. It gives 40 more fish in 10 years.
maths.explain: At 18 fish the village can take 9 a year, which is 90 in 10 years. At 30 fish they can take only 5 a year, which is 50. 90 − 50 = 40.
maths.context: This is about the Fishing Rule, where a table tells you how many new fish a pond adds at each size.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two rules over many years shows which one really gives more, when the first year can mislead.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out why hunters and hunted rise and fall in waves? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out to be too simple.
how_we_found_out.story: During the First World War, fishing in the Adriatic Sea almost stopped. Afterwards the Italian biologist Umberto D'Ancona studied the fish market records. He found that sharks and other hunting fish had become a larger share of the catch. He asked his father-in-law, the mathematician Vito Volterra, why. In 1926 Volterra wrote two equations, one for the hunted and one for the hunters. They gave two waves that rise and fall for ever. Alfred Lotka in America had written the same equations a little earlier. Many people then believed that any hunter and prey kept together would swing like this. In Moscow, Georgy Gause tested the idea in glass tubes with two tiny pond animals. There were no waves. The hunters ate all the prey and starved. Waves appeared only when he added a few new animals every few days. In 1958 Carl Huffaker got three waves from mites on oranges, but only on a large, patchy tray.
how_we_found_out.who: Umberto D'Ancona and Vito Volterra in Italy, Alfred Lotka in the United States, Georgy Gause in Moscow, and Carl Huffaker in California.
how_we_found_out.when: 1925 and 1926 (the equations), 1934 (Gause's book The Struggle for Existence) and 1958 (Huffaker's mites)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a hunter and the hunted, kept together, will always rise and fall in waves, as the equations say. Gause's tubes showed that in a small, simple space the hunters eat everything and both die out. Waves need hiding places, distance or new arrivals.
how_we_found_out.art: A glass tube of water with tiny animals in it beside a tray of oranges, and above them a graph of two wavy lines.

roots.context: We have learned that every population stops growing at a limit set by the place its members live in. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Full Island Test, every tree dropped one seed in every round, from first to last. The forest still stopped at 36 trees, and at 18 on the half island. No tree chose that number, and no tree changed what they did. How many there are of any living being is not decided inside that being. It is set by what the place can give to all of them together.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'there are 3,682 tigers' as if the number belonged to tigers, the way stripes do. But the number belongs to the forests, the deer and the tigers together. Change the place and the number changes, with the same animals.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Full Island Test the rule for the trees never changed. Yet the forest levelled off at 36 on the full island and near 18 on the half island. In India, the number of tigers in a forest follows the number of their prey.

three.who_am_i: You are one of about 8 billion people. That number, like the 36 trees, is held up by soil, rain, sunlight and other living beings.
three.what_is_life: Every living being can multiply without end, and none ever does. Life is always pressing against what the place can give.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not a box that living beings fill. The beings and the place set each other's numbers, as the rats and the snakes did.

roots.thread: One bacterium becomes two, two become four, and so the one becomes many. But the many never become endless. The sunlight, water and atoms of one place are shared out among all who live there. So each population's number is its share of one supply. When one number rises, others must fall. Counting any one species is really measuring a part of the whole place.

teachings.teaching: The life of a person who lives without knowing their measure may look as if it is doing well. Then it is gone, and nothing is left to show for it.
teachings.link: Valluvar wrote this about a person's wealth. The reindeer of St Matthew Island lived it. The herd looked as if it was thriving until the year it vanished, because it had gone past the measure of the island.

teachings.teaching: The way of nature is like the bending of a bow. The high end is brought down and the low end is raised. What has too much is reduced, and what has too little is added to.
teachings.link: This is how a crowded population and a sparse one behave. In a crowd, deaths rise and births fall. Where members are few, each has plenty and the number grows. Both are pulled toward the carrying capacity.

science.text: Populations in closed spaces level off at a carrying capacity, and crowding raises deaths or lowers births (Verhulst, 1838; Gause, 1934).
Bacteria sense how crowded they are through chemical signals and change what they do together (Nealson, Platt and Hastings, 1970; Bassler and others).
Whether the Earth has a carrying capacity for people, and what it is, depends on how people live (Cohen, 1995).

other_view.view: A population's number is only a sum. Each animal eats, breeds and dies on their own account, and nothing is shared out or held together. 'The place sets the number' is a short way of describing millions of separate lives. Charvaka thinkers of ancient India would agree: only the separate things we can see are real, and the whole is just a word.

practice.title: The feeling of enough
practice.say: Sit with a tumbler of water. Take one small sip and wait for one breath. Take another sip, and wait again. Keep going slowly. Notice the moment when your body says that is enough. You did not count the sips. Your body sensed its own limit. A population finds its limit in the same way, by sensing, not by counting.
practice.kid: Sit with a tumbler of water. Take one small sip. Wait for one breath. Sip again and wait again. Notice when your body says enough. You did not count. Your body knew.

ask: The forest stopped at 36 though no tree decided to stop. So who or what decided?
Your family eats rice grown in a field far away. Is that field part of the place that carries you?
If the number of tigers belongs to the forest and the deer too, what are we saving when we 'save the tiger'?
People can choose how much each of us uses. Does that make our limit different from a deer's limit, or the same?

playtest: The experiments, games and activities in this lesson were reasoned through step by step, and two were run many times on a computer. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat the amounts and times as a starting point. The Full Island Test (core) needs paper, a ruler, two dice and about 40 beans. A computer ran its rule 2,000 times: the forest reached 34 to 36 trees by round 8 or 9 on the full island, and 17 or 18 by round 8 on the half island. The late rounds have about 30 rolls each, so work as a pair. The Rats and Snakes Game was run 400 times on a computer with these sizes. Most games show the rats filling the field, then the snakes rising, then both falling, which is about one and a half waves in 14 rounds. Real tosses are less even than a computer's, so your graph may be more ragged. If the snakes die out round after round, toss from a little closer. In Doubling Rice, the square where the grains stop fitting depends on your rice. In Count Without Counting, use pale beans so the ink dot shows, and stir well. Crowded Cups takes three weeks, and the cups often look alike for the first week. If the crowded cup grows mould, that is a result, not a failure. The Meadow Game was run 4,000 times for each herd size: keeping 6 to 8 chital scored best, about 26 to 28 on average. In the Fishing Rule, every total in the notes was checked by working the table through. Fewer Mosquitoes needs a grown-up for the roof, tanks and outdoors. No core part needs a garden. Facts checked online on 18 Nov 2026: the St Matthew Island counts, Gause's and Huffaker's results, the Krebs study of 1995, the Karanth study of 2004, the 2022 tiger estimate, the Kaziranga rhino counts, the Eravikulam tahr counts and closure months, the United Nations forecast, India's fertility figure, the 1970 quorum sensing paper, Sprengel and Liebig, Cohen's range of estimates, Thirukkural 479 and Tao Te Ching 77. Both teachings are given in our own plain words. Not checked online, and given from standard references: the years in which the world passed 1 to 7 billion, the thrips study of Andrewartha, the books of Malthus, Boserup and Meadows, and the lengths of two of the videos. The story's people and their words are imagined.
